title: Ultrametricity of Energy Minimum Configurations of RNA Secondary Structures in the Nussinov Model
summary: We present a numerical study of the ultrametric properties of the set of RNA secondary structures with the maximum number of base pairs (energetically degenerate minima) within the maximum matching model (Nussinov algorithm). Using 18 natural small nuclear RNAs as examples, we show that the degree of nontrivial ultrametricity varies widely. We consider the optimization problem for the degree of nontrivial ultrametricity of RNA secondary structures with the maximum number of base pairs under a fixed nucleotide composition. It is found that permuting the nucleotide sequence can strongly change the degree of ultrametricity, indicating the key role of nucleotide order in shaping the hierarchical properties of RNA secondary structures.

AI.tldr: This paper numerically studies the ultrametric properties of energetically degenerate RNA secondary structures (maximum base pairs) using the Nussinov algorithm, showing that ultrametricity varies across 18 natural snRNAs and that nucleotide order (not just composition) strongly influences hierarchical structure.
AI.motivation: To understand the hierarchical (ultrametric) properties of RNA secondary structures that share the same maximum number of base pairs, and to investigate how nucleotide sequence order vs. composition affects these properties.
AI.method: Numerical study using the maximum matching model (Nussinov algorithm) on 18 natural small nuclear RNAs; analysis of ultrametricity degree; optimization of nucleotide sequence permutation to alter ultrametric properties.
AI.result: The degree of nontrivial ultrametricity varies widely among the 18 RNAs; permuting nucleotide sequences strongly changes the degree of ultrametricity, demonstrating that nucleotide order plays a key role.
AI.conclusion: Nucleotide order, not just composition, is a critical determinant of the hierarchical properties of RNA secondary structure landscapes.

title: Relationship between heat effects and shear modulus relaxation during structural relaxation of a telluride glass
summary: We performed parallel measurements of heat effects and shear modulus relaxation for glassy Te$_{75}$Ge$_{15}$Ga$_{10}$ taken as a representative of practically important non-metallic glasses with covalent bonding. It is shown that the heat effects occurring upon heating are quantitatively linked to the shear moduli in the glassy and crystalline states and their temperature derivatives as implied by Eq.(1), which was originally derived for metallic glasses. This relationship provides a good description of exo- and endothermal reactions using shear modulus relaxation data as an input. This is the first application of this approach to a non-metallic glass with directional interatomic bonding. The obtained results suggest that relaxation phenomena are governed by elastic dipoles -- atomic configurations with the symmetry lower than that of surrounding matrix.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that the quantitative link between heat effects and shear modulus relaxation (originally developed for metallic glasses) also applies to non-metallic covalent glass Te₇₅Ge₁₅Ga₁₀, supporting the elastic dipole model for relaxation phenomena.
AI.motivation: To test whether the established relationship between heat effects and shear modulus relaxation, previously validated for metallic glasses, holds for non-metallic glasses with covalent directional bonding.
AI.method: Parallel measurements of heat effects and shear modulus relaxation were performed on glassy Te₇₅Ge₁₅Ga₁₀. The data were analyzed using Eq.(1) (originally derived for metallic glasses) which links heat effects to shear moduli in glassy and crystalline states and their temperature derivatives.
AI.result: The relationship quantitatively describes both exo- and endothermal reactions using shear modulus relaxation data as input. This is the first successful application to a non-metallic glass with directional interatomic bonding.
AI.conclusion: Relaxation phenomena in glasses are governed by elastic dipoles — atomic configurations with lower symmetry than the surrounding matrix — consistent with the elastic dipole model.

title: Locally resolved electronic textures of reconstruction domains in marginally twisted monolayer-bilayer graphene
summary: Controlling the stacking and rotational registry of graphene layers provides a powerful handle on atomic-scale structural reconstructions that alter the electronic landscape at the nanoscale. In particular, this governs how massless and massive Dirac fermions coexist and interact at the monolayer-bilayer graphene interface. In the limit of marginal twist, the system reconstructs into domains of distinct vertical stacking order, introducing characteristic electronic properties and new electronic length scales, a regime that, despite its structural richness, remains largely unexplored. Here, using scanning tunnelling microscopy and spectroscopy, we demonstrate that at very low rotation angles the monolayer-bilayer graphene system relaxes into a network of three distinct stacking domains with individual electronic textures revealed through spatially resolved spectroscopic mapping and corroborated by computed local density of states. We report switching of the hierarchy of the tunnelling characteristics between Bernal and rhombohedral domains as a function of bias voltage. Furthermore, the measured spectroscopic maps exhibit theoretically anticipated domain wall 'twirling' around energetically unfavorable AAB stacking nodes, promoted by out-of-plane deformations. Our results shed light on fundamental structure-property relationships underpinning moiré-driven phenomena, opening new avenues for harnessing structural degrees of freedom in van der Waals heterostructures.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how low-angle twist in monolayer-bilayer graphene leads to structural reconstruction into three distinct stacking domains, revealing bias-dependent switching of electronic properties and domain wall "twirling" around AAB nodes, as observed via STM/STS and corroborated by LDOS calculations.
AI.motivation: To explore the largely unexplored regime of marginal twist in monolayer-bilayer graphene, where structural reconstruction introduces new electronic length scales and governs the coexistence of massless and massive Dirac fermions.
AI.method: Scanning tunnelling microscopy and spectroscopy (STM/STS) combined with computed local density of states (LDOS) to probe spatially resolved electronic textures of reconstructed stacking domains.
AI.result: Identification of three distinct stacking domains with unique electronic signatures; bias-dependent switching of tunnelling hierarchy between Bernal and rhombohedral domains; observation of domain wall "twirling" around AAB stacking nodes driven by out-of-plane deformations.
AI.conclusion: The results elucidate fundamental structure-property relationships in moiré-driven phenomena and open new avenues for exploiting structural degrees of freedom in van der Waals heterostructures.

title: Conserving relaxation-time approximation for electron-electron collisions
summary: We develop a conserving relaxation-time approximation (cRTA), which explicitly enforces conservation of particle number, energy, and momentum and employs an energy-resolved projection onto the full space of collision invariants. This makes the cRTA applicable to transport quantities sensitive to the energy dependence of the nonequilibrium quasiparticle distribution near the Fermi surface. We benchmark the cRTA against several exact and asymptotically exact results. In particular, it reproduces the low- and high-temperature limits of the dc conductivity of a non-Galilean-invariant Fermi liquid (FL) with disorder, the hydrodynamic and collisionless limits of the finite wavevector longitudinal conductivity of a clean Galilean-invariant FL, and the asymptotic scaling forms of the optical conductivity of a clean non-Galilean-invariant FL beyond the semiclassical limit. For several observables, the agreement with exact solutions is quantitative at the percent level. These results demonstrate that the cRTA provides a simple and accurate framework for transport beyond the Fermi surface projection approximation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a conserving relaxation-time approximation (cRTA) that enforces conservation laws and uses energy-resolved projection onto collision invariants, benchmarked against exact results for Fermi liquid transport, achieving percent-level accuracy.
AI.motivation: Standard relaxation-time approximations violate conservation laws and fail to capture energy-dependent transport near the Fermi surface. The authors aim to develop a simple yet accurate framework that respects particle number, energy, and momentum conservation while being applicable to nontrivial transport phenomena beyond the semiclassical limit.
AI.method: The cRTA enforces explicit conservation of particle number, energy, and momentum via an energy-resolved projection onto the full space of collision invariants. It is benchmarked against exact and asymptotically exact results for Fermi liquids, including dc conductivity with disorder, finite wavevector longitudinal conductivity, and optical conductivity.
AI.result: The cRTA reproduces low- and high-temperature limits of dc conductivity for non-Galilean-invariant FLs with disorder, hydrodynamic and collisionless limits of conductivity in clean Galilean-invariant FLs, and asymptotic scaling of optical conductivity beyond the semiclassical limit. Agreement with exact solutions is quantitative at the percent level.
AI.conclusion: The cRTA provides a simple, accurate framework for transport beyond the Fermi surface projection approximation, maintaining conservation laws while achieving near-exact accuracy for a range of observables.

title: Taming non-equilibrium thermal fluctuations in subthreshold CMOS circuits
summary: As CMOS technology scales down, thermal fluctuations increasingly impact circuit behavior, posing challenges to conventional circuit design. However, the inherent stochasticity introduced by thermal noise is now being explored as a potential resource in the emerging field of probabilistic computing. This work presents a fully CMOS experimental platform that enables direct control over its intrinsic thermal fluctuations. These devices function as programmable multivariate Gaussian samplers, offering a hardware primitive for energy-efficient stochastic computing and serving as an experimental platform for studies in electronic noise and stochastic thermodynamics.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a fully CMOS experimental platform that enables direct control over intrinsic thermal fluctuations, functioning as programmable multivariate Gaussian samplers for energy-efficient stochastic computing and experimental studies in electronic noise and stochastic thermodynamics.
AI.motivation: Thermal fluctuations in scaled CMOS technology pose challenges to conventional circuit design, but the authors explore leveraging these inherent stochasticity as a resource for probabilistic computing rather than treating it as a problem.
AI.method: The authors develop a fully CMOS experimental platform that allows direct control over its intrinsic thermal fluctuations, functioning as programmable multivariate Gaussian samplers.
AI.result: The platform enables programmable multivariate Gaussian sampling, providing a hardware primitive for energy-efficient stochastic computing and an experimental platform for studies in electronic noise and stochastic thermodynamics.
AI.conclusion: Thermal noise, traditionally a challenge in CMOS scaling, can be harnessed as a resource for probabilistic computing via a fully CMOS platform that controls intrinsic fluctuations for energy-efficient stochastic computation and fundamental noise studies.

title: AutoDFT: A Closed-Loop Multi-Agent Framework for Autonomous DFT Calculations
summary: Density functional theory (DFT) serves as the basis for computational discovery in materials science and chemistry, yet each calculation demands extensive human effort: adjusting algorithms when convergence stalls, revising plans when unexpected physics emerges, and inserting steps as intermediate results reshape the problem. Existing LLM-based agents automate only the initial planning stage, producing a full execution plan upfront and leaving all subsequent adaptation to hand-crafted rules. As a result, these workflows remain fragile, do not generalize well beyond pre-planned scenarios, and often require expert intervention when failures or unexpected intermediate results require changes to the calculation path. Here, we introduce AutoDFT, a closed-loop multi-agent framework that embeds LLM reasoning into every stage of the DFT lifecycle, where a strategic planner produces a skeletal plan of step objectives; a step planner generates numerical parameters just in time from preceding results; and a monitor-recover-reflect cycle diagnoses failures, repairs them, and revises the plan when the evidence justifies it. We demonstrate both breadth and depth: breadth on VASPBench, a purpose-built benchmark spanning 34 tasks and 9 DFT calculation types, where AutoDFT achieves 94.1% task-level success with GPT-5.2; and depth on established materials databases, where AutoDFT produces quantitatively reliable property predictions across electronic, magnetic, and energetic properties. By closing the loop between planning and execution, AutoDFT enables experimentalists without deep computational expertise to obtain reliable first-principles results.

AI.tldr: AutoDFT is a closed-loop multi-agent LLM framework that integrates reasoning into every stage of DFT calculations—strategic planning, just-in-time step planning, and a monitor-recover-reflect cycle—achieving 94.1% task success on VASPBench and reliable property predictions across diverse materials properties, enabling non-experts to run first-principles computations.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based agents for DFT automate only initial planning, producing static execution plans that cannot adapt to convergence failures, unexpected physics, or intermediate results, requiring frequent expert intervention and limiting generalization.
AI.method: AutoDFT is a closed-loop multi-agent framework with three components: (1) a strategic planner that generates a skeletal plan of step objectives, (2) a step planner that produces numerical parameters just in time from preceding results, and (3) a monitor-recover-reflect cycle that diagnoses failures, repairs them, and revises the plan when warranted.
AI.result: 94.1% task-level success on VASPBench (34 tasks, 9 calculation types) with GPT-5.2, and quantitatively reliable predictions of electronic, magnetic, and energetic properties on established materials databases.
AI.conclusion: By closing the loop between planning and execution, AutoDFT enables experimentalists without deep computational expertise to obtain reliable first-principles results.

title: Selective Biexciton Generation Under Energy-Time Entangled Quantum Light in Quantum Dots
summary: Energy-time entangled photons provide new opportunities for controlling multiphoton absorption beyond classical limits. Here, we investigate biexciton generation in nanocrystal quantum dots driven by energy-time-entangled quantum light generated via a spontaneous parametric down-conversion process. We show that quantum correlations can enhance biexciton production while suppressing excitonic populations. By employing a three-level model, we demonstrate that biexciton generation depends nontrivially on the photon arrival-time entanglement and the pump bandwidth. Consequently, we find that maximizing efficiency requires an optimally shaped entangled photon field rather than simply scaling parameters for a monotonic improvement. Extending to a realistic CdSe/CdS core-shell quantum dots containing many excitonic states coupled to the quantum field, we demonstrate that increasing the bi-photon arrival time entanglement (closer arrival time) enhances constructive pathway interference and expands accessible excitation channels while preserving a better energy conservation excitation than classical light when generating biexciton. Furthermore, tuning the time correlation properties enables selective excitation of closely spaced biexciton states. These results establish entangled quantum light as a powerful tool for selective excitation and control of nonlinear optical processes in quantum-confined systems.

AI.tldr: Energy-time entangled photons can enhance biexciton generation while suppressing excitonic populations in quantum dots, with optimal efficiency requiring shaped entangled fields and tunable time correlations enabling selective state excitation.
AI.motivation: To investigate how energy-time entangled quantum light can control multiphoton absorption beyond classical limits, specifically for biexciton generation in nanocrystal quantum dots.
AI.method: Uses a three-level model and extends to realistic CdSe/CdS core-shell quantum dots with many excitonic states, analyzing biexciton generation under energy-time-entangled light from SPDC, with tunable photon arrival-time entanglement and pump bandwidth.
AI.result: Quantum correlations enhance biexciton production while suppressing excitonic populations; maximizing efficiency requires optimally shaped entangled fields; increasing arrival-time entanglement enhances constructive pathway interference and expands excitation channels; tuning time correlations enables selective excitation of closely spaced biexciton states.
AI.conclusion: Entangled quantum light is a powerful tool for selective excitation and control of nonlinear optical processes in quantum-confined systems.

title: Slave-boson Formalism for Superconducting Pairing at Strong Coupling
summary: We study the emergence of superconductivity in the one-band Hubbard model using the spin-rotation-invariant Kotliar-Ruckenstein slave-boson (SB) approach. Motivated by its intrinsically renormalized mean-field ground state, we construct an effective pairing vertex from dynamical fluctuations about the saddle point. Solving the anisotropic, frequency-dependent gap equation on the square lattice, we map the pairing instabilities across doping, interaction, temperature and real-frequency gap structure that qualitatively match experimental cuprate observations. This framework merges strong-correlation SB-type renormalizations with RPA-type pairing transparency, providing a scalable route to modeling multi-orbital superconductivity at strong coupling.

AI.tldr: Using a spin-rotation-invariant slave-boson approach, the paper studies superconductivity in the one-band Hubbard model by constructing an effective pairing vertex from dynamical fluctuations around a renormalized mean-field saddle point. Solving the anisotropic gap equation yields pairing instabilities across doping, interaction, temperature, and real-frequency gap structure that match cuprate observations, merging strong-correlation SB renormalizations with RPA-like pairing transparency.
AI.motivation: To develop a framework that bridges strong-correlation slave-boson renormalizations with transparent RPA-type pairing analysis, enabling scalable modeling of superconductivity in strongly correlated systems, particularly the cuprates.
AI.method: Spin-rotation-invariant Kotliar-Ruckenstein slave-boson approach; dynamical fluctuations about the saddle point construct an effective pairing vertex; solved as an anisotropic, frequency-dependent gap equation on the square lattice.
AI.result: Mapping of pairing instabilities across doping, interaction strength, temperature, and real-frequency gap structure that qualitatively match experimental observations in cuprate superconductors.
AI.conclusion: The SB+RPA hybrid framework successfully captures cuprate superconductivity phenomenology and offers a scalable route to modeling multi-orbital superconductivity at strong coupling.

title: Chips in the Flatland : 2D Semiconductors for Future Computing Electronic
summary: As transistor scaling approaches its fundamental physical limits in the Angstrom era, two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors have emerged as the promising channel material candidates for future computing. While the device physics of 2D semiconductors have been rigorously explored, translating these nanodevices into fully functional integrated circuits remains a largely uncharted frontier. This review bridges the gap between material- and device-centric breakthroughs and circuit-level chip design in 2D semiconductors, a valley of death that has so far prevented translation of high-performance individual transistors into functional chips. We track the evolution of 2D semi-conductor field-effect transistors from basic Boolean logic families and standard cells to complex chip architectures, including recent milestones in RISC-V and monolithic CMOS microprocessors. Critically, we highlight the indispensable role of multiscale compact modeling, spanning semiclassical, quantum-hybrid and data-driven approaches, as the necessary link between device physics and the electronic design automation workflows for scalable chip development. By summarizing recent breakthroughs and identifying the bottlenecks in both fab and fabless trajectories of 2D semiconductors, this review shall provide insights that motivates the translation of proof-of-concept 2D transistors into fully functional computing chips, paving a way towards future Angstrom era computing technology empowered by 2D semiconductors.

AI.tldr: This review bridges the gap between 2D semiconductor device-level breakthroughs and circuit-level chip design, covering the evolution from basic logic families to complex architectures like RISC-V and CMOS microprocessors, with emphasis on multiscale compact modeling as the critical link for scalable chip development.
AI.motivation: Despite rigorous exploration of 2D semiconductor device physics, translating these nanodevices into fully functional integrated circuits remains largely uncharted, creating a "valley of death" between high-performance individual transistors and functional chips.
AI.method: The review tracks the evolution of 2D semiconductor FETs from Boolean logic families and standard cells to complex chip architectures (RISC-V, monolithic CMOS microprocessors), highlighting multiscale compact modeling (semiclassical, quantum-hybrid, data-driven) as the link between device physics and EDA workflows.
AI.result: Summarizes recent breakthroughs in 2D semiconductor integrated circuits and identifies bottlenecks in both fab and fabless development trajectories toward functional computing chips.
AI.conclusion: Multiscale compact modeling is indispensable for scalable chip development, and addressing current bottlenecks will enable translation of proof-of-concept 2D transistors into fully functional chips for Angstrom-era computing.

title: MARUT: An Exascale-Ready, GPU-Accelerated High-Order CFD Framework with AMR for High-Speed Flows and Finite-Rate Chemistry
summary: We present \texttt{MARUT}, a scalable multi-GPU computational fluid dynamics (CFD) framework designed for high-fidelity simulations of compressible flows spanning subsonic to hypersonic regimes, including chemically reacting nonequilibrium flows with finite-rate chemistry and adaptive mesh refinement (AMR). The framework addresses a central challenge in contemporary scientific computing: the development of numerically accurate and computationally scalable algorithms capable of resolving strongly nonlinear, multiscale flow physics on emerging heterogeneous supercomputing architectures. Built around a distributed-memory MPI-parallel infrastructure and implemented natively on NVIDIA GPUs, \texttt{MARUT} combines high-order spectral discontinuous Galerkin discretisations with strong-stability-preserving Runge--Kutta time integration to achieve low-dissipation and high-resolution representation of shocks, vortical structures and reactive interfaces. Dynamic AMR further enables efficient concentration of computational resources in localized regions of physical complexity, thereby substantially reducing computational cost while preserving solution fidelity. \texttt{MARUT} is designed to maintain strong parallel efficiency through GPU-resident computations and scalable MPI communication strategies, achieving near-linear strong scaling across multiple GPUs. The solver is validated against a broad suite of canonical benchmark problems involving inviscid and reactive compressible flows, including subsonic, transonic, supersonic and hypersonic configurations with multi-species nonequilibrium chemistry, where the numerical predictions show close agreement with established reference solutions. Beyond its immediate performance characteristics, the framework reflects the broader transition of computational science towards modular, adaptive and AI-compatible simulation ecosystems.

AI.tldr: MARUT is a scalable multi-GPU CFD framework for high-fidelity compressible flow simulations (subsonic to hypersonic) with finite-rate chemistry and AMR, using high-order DG discretizations and RK time integration, achieving near-linear strong scaling on NVIDIA GPUs.
AI.motivation: To address the challenge of developing numerically accurate and computationally scalable algorithms for strongly nonlinear, multiscale flow physics on emerging heterogeneous supercomputing architectures, enabling high-fidelity simulation of compressible flows including chemically reacting nonequilibrium flows.
AI.method: Combines distributed-memory MPI-parallel infrastructure with native GPU implementation, high-order spectral discontinuous Galerkin discretizations, strong-stability-preserving Runge–Kutta time integration, and dynamic AMR.
AI.result: Achieves near-linear strong scaling across multiple GPUs with strong parallel efficiency; validated against canonical benchmarks from subsonic to hypersonic regimes including multi-species nonequilibrium chemistry, showing close agreement with reference solutions.
AI.conclusion: MARUT demonstrates that modular, adaptive, and AI-compatible simulation ecosystems represent the broader transition in computational science, enabling efficient high-fidelity simulations on heterogeneous architectures.

title: Parity non-conservation in isotope chain of tin
summary: We calculate parity non-conservation (PNC) amplitudes for all magnetic-dipole (M1) transitions within the ground $5p^2$ configuration of Sn. Among the transitions considered, the $^1$S$_0$-$^3$P$_1$ transition has the largest PNC amplitude and appears to be the most promising candidate for experiment. We also discuss a measurement method capable of achieving unprecedentedly high precision in a measurement of PNC in this transition. We argue that the most robust test should be based on ratios of PNC amplitudes for different isotopes, since the atomic-structure factor largely cancels in such ratios. We study the effect of the neutron skin on these isotope ratios using available nuclear data for Sn and show that the uncertainty associated with the neutron skin can be reduced to the $10^{-3}$ level relative to the isotopic variation of the PNC effect. Our results indicate that PNC measurements along a chain of Sn isotopes offer a realistic and sensitive probe of new physics.

AI.tldr: The paper calculates parity non-conservation (PNC) amplitudes for M1 transitions in the ground $5p^2$ configuration of Sn, identifies the $^1$S$_0$-$^3$P$_1$ transition as the most promising candidate, proposes a high-precision measurement method, and shows that isotope ratio measurements can probe new physics with neutron skin uncertainty reduced to $10^{-3}$ level.
AI.motivation: To identify promising atomic transitions in Sn for parity non-conservation measurements that can serve as sensitive probes of new physics beyond the Standard Model.
AI.method: Calculated PNC amplitudes for all M1 transitions within the ground $5p^2$ configuration of Sn; proposed a high-precision measurement method; used isotope ratios to cancel atomic-structure factors; incorporated nuclear neutron skin data to quantify uncertainties.
AI.result: The $^1$S$_0$-$^3$P$_1$ transition has the largest PNC amplitude; neutron skin uncertainty can be reduced to $10^{-3}$ level relative to isotopic variation of the PNC effect.
AI.conclusion: PNC measurements along a chain of Sn isotopes offer a realistic and sensitive probe of new physics.

title: Anharmonic Quantum Transport Analysis of Thermal Transport Anomalies in Ultrathin Silicon Nanowires
summary: Thermal transport in low-dimensional semiconductors is crucial for advancing thermal management in nanoelectronics, quantum devices, and thermoelectric devices. Recent molecular dynamics (MD) studies have identified a nonmonotonic dependence of thermal conductivity (k) on diameter in ultrathin silicon nanowires (NWs). However, classical MD methods are limited at low temperatures and in strongly confined regimes. This work introduces a fully quantum-mechanical perspective on this anomaly by employing anharmonic non-equilibrium Green's function (NEGF) simulations combined with density-functional-theory-trained neuroevolution potentials. For [001]- and [110]-oriented NWs, k decreases with diameter d to a minimum at d_c = 6.24 nm and 5.50 nm, respectively, then rises with d, for a temperature range of 10-300 K. At room temperature, this behavior arises from dominant momentum-conserving normal scattering relative to Umklapp processes in confined regimes, thereby enabling Poiseuille-like hydrodynamic phonon flow that competes with boundary scattering. At cryogenic temperatures, strong radial confinement quantizes the phonon spectrum, and only low-frequency phonons (< 2 THz) significantly contribute to heat transport through quasi-ballistic propagation of long-wavelength modes, as demonstrated by the spectral thermal conductance. In contrast to classical MD, which is inaccurate at low temperatures due to overexcitation of high-frequency vibrations by Boltzmann statistics, neglect of quantum suppression, and overestimation of thermal conductivity in thinner NWs with stronger quantum confinement, the NEGF framework provides quantitative accuracy even at low temperatures, such as 10 K.

AI.tldr: This work uses anharmonic non-equilibrium Green's function (NEGF) simulations with neuroevolution potentials to reveal a nonmonotonic diameter dependence of thermal conductivity in ultrathin silicon nanowires, explained by Poiseuille-like hydrodynamic phonon flow at room temperature and quantum-confinement-induced spectral quantization at cryogenic temperatures, with NEGF providing quantitative accuracy where classical MD fails.
AI.motivation: Understanding thermal transport in low-dimensional semiconductors is critical for nanoelectronics, quantum devices, and thermoelectrics. Classical MD studies identified a nonmonotonic k vs. diameter anomaly in SiNWs but are fundamentally limited at low temperatures and in strongly confined regimes due to Boltzmann statistics, neglect of quantum suppression, and overestimation of k in thinner NWs.
AI.method: Anharmonic non-equilibrium Green's function (NEGF) simulations combined with density-functional-theory-trained neuroevolution potentials, applied to [001]- and [110]-oriented silicon nanowires over 10–300 K and varying diameters.
AI.result: k decreases with d to a minimum (d_c = 6.24 nm for [001], 5.50 nm for [110]), then rises. At 300 K, Poiseuille-like hydrodynamic phonon flow from dominant normal scattering competes with boundary scattering. At cryogenic temperatures, radial confinement quantizes the phonon spectrum; only <2 THz modes contribute via quasi-ballistic transport. NEGF achieves quantitative accuracy even at 10 K, unlike classical MD.
AI.conclusion: The NEGF framework provides a fully quantum-mechanical perspective that quantitatively resolves the nonmonotonic k-diameter anomaly in SiNWs across all temperatures, overcoming classical MD limitations. This establishes NEGF as a reliable tool for nanoscale thermal transport in strongly confined quantum regimes.

title: Quantum Interference Corrections in Electron Hydrodynamics
summary: We show that quantum-interference corrections in an electron fluid are tightly constrained by hydrodynamic Ward identities: charge and momentum conservation protect the $m=0,\pm1$ sectors, so the leading correction first appears in the spin-two $m=\pm2$ stress sector. The resulting hydrodynamic Cooperon has a robust infrared structure that renormalizes stress relaxation, and hence the viscosity. In channel flow this lowers the viscous resistivity, producing a hydrodynamic interference signature with the opposite sign to ordinary weak localization.

AI.tldr: Quantum-interference corrections in an electron fluid are constrained by hydrodynamic Ward identities, with the leading correction appearing in the spin-two stress sector, renormalizing viscosity and producing a hydrodynamic interference signature opposite to ordinary weak localization.
AI.motivation: To understand how quantum-interference corrections behave in an electron fluid under hydrodynamic constraints, and to identify signatures that distinguish this regime from ordinary weak localization.
AI.method: The authors apply hydrodynamic Ward identities (charge and momentum conservation) to analyze quantum-interference corrections, showing they protect the m=0,±1 sectors while the leading correction emerges in the m=±2 stress sector via a hydrodynamic Cooperon.
AI.result: The hydrodynamic Cooperon renormalizes stress relaxation and viscosity. In channel flow, this lowers viscous resistivity, producing an interference signature with opposite sign compared to ordinary weak localization.
AI.conclusion: Quantum-interference corrections in electron fluids are governed by hydrodynamic constraints, leading to distinct viscocity renormalization and a unique hydrodynamic interference signature.

title: Multi-Scale Coherence of Represented Flows
summary: Many problems in nonlinear and statistical physics are formulated through represented flows, including physical-space vector fields, phase-space drift fields, and truncated renormalization-group beta functions. We introduce a complementary representation-dependent diagnostic for testing whether finite-separation flow geometry is stable across observational resolution. For two separated points, states, or theories, the method compares the direction of the corresponding vector-field increment after the field has been smoothed at two resolutions. Averaging this normalized comparison over sampled separations gives a coherence matrix tied to the chosen variables, coarse graining, metric, and sampling protocol; it is a consistency test, not a coordinate-invariant quantity. We demonstrate the diagnostic in three settings. Synthetic divergence-free fields with identical Fourier amplitudes, spectra, and scalar two-point correlations nevertheless produce distinct coherence matrices, showing that second-order statistics do not determine cross-resolution increment geometry. Lorenz phase-space tests show that a smooth coordinate wrinkling changes represented drift geometry without changing the underlying dynamics, and that a weak model perturbation lowers finite-separation coherence even when local stretching proxies remain closely matched. Finally, for functional renormalization-group flows of the three-dimensional \(O(1)\) scalar theory, projected \(M=4,5,6\) LPA beta fields remain internally coherent, while cross-truncation coherence decreases as higher-order coupling directions are activated. The diagnostic provides a practical field-level check of how representations, models, and truncations preserve finite-separation flow geometry, complementing rather than replacing standard local, spectral, or fixed-point diagnostics.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a representation-dependent diagnostic that tests whether finite-separation flow geometry is stable across observational resolutions, demonstrated on synthetic vector fields, Lorenz phase-space flows, and functional RG flows of the 3D O(1) scalar theory.
AI.motivation: Standard local, spectral, and fixed-point diagnostics are insufficient to determine whether finite-separation flow geometry is preserved across different observational resolutions, motivating a complementary consistency test tied to specific representations and coarse-graining protocols.
AI.method: The method compares the direction of vector-field increments at two resolutions for separated points, averaged over sampled separations to form a coherence matrix; it is applied to synthetic divergence-free fields, Lorenz phase-space tests with coordinate wrinkling and model perturbation, and functional RG beta fields under LPA truncations.
AI.result: Synthetic fields with identical second-order statistics produce distinct coherence matrices; coordinate wrinkling changes represented drift geometry without altering dynamics; weak model perturbation lowers coherence despite matched stretching proxies; projected LPA beta fields remain internally coherent but cross-truncation coherence decreases as higher-order couplings activate.
AI.conclusion: The coherence diagnostic provides a practical field-level check for how representations, models, and truncations preserve finite-separation flow geometry, complementing existing diagnostics without replacing them.

title: Diamond compound refractive lenses for high energy Dark Field X-ray Microscopy
summary: Compound-refractive lenses (CRL) are a type of x-ray optics that find widespread applications as focusing and imaging lenses. The choice of material is one of the most defining properties of these lenses. In this work, we present a CRL made out of diamond. It provides an advantageous balance between refractivity and absorption, along with good manufacturability. Compared to Be CRLs, it features a higher optical density and thus enables application at higher photon energies without relying on large lens stacks or very small radii of curvature, which are challenging to manufacture. A diamond CRL is characterized for use as an objective for Dark-field X-ray Microscopy (DFXM) at the ID03 beamline of the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility (ESRF) and compared to Al and Be CRLs at 17 keV, 33 keV and 37 keV. Increasing the photon energy in DFXM from 17 keV to 37 keV opens up the possibility to investigate new sample systems, that were previously opaque to low energy x-ray radiation. The capability of the diamond CRL at 33 keV is illustrated through DFXM measurements on two 0.5 mm-thick iron-based samples, which cannot be probed at 17 keV.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a diamond compound-refractive lens (CRL) for X-ray microscopy, demonstrating its superior performance at higher photon energies (17-37 keV) compared to conventional Al and Be CRLs, and showing its effectiveness for Dark-field X-ray Microscopy (DFXM) on thick iron-based samples that are opaque to lower energy X-rays.
AI.motivation: To develop a CRL material that balances refractivity and absorption while enabling operation at higher photon energies without requiring large lens stacks or very small radii of curvature, thus allowing investigation of sample systems previously opaque to low-energy X-ray radiation.
AI.method: A diamond CRL was fabricated and characterized as an objective for Dark-field X-ray Microscopy (DFXM) at the ID03 beamline of the ESRF, and compared to Al and Be CRLs at 17 keV, 33 keV, and 37 keV photon energies.
AI.result: The diamond CRL enables operation at higher photon energies (up to 37 keV) with favorable optical density. DFXM measurements on 0.5 mm-thick iron-based samples were successfully performed at 33 keV, which cannot be probed at 17 keV.
AI.conclusion: Diamond CRLs offer an advantageous balance of properties for high-energy X-ray microscopy, particularly enabling DFXM studies of thick, previously opaque samples at energies up to 37 keV.

title: Superconductivity-enhanced phonon angular momentum
summary: We theoretically investigate the properties of phonon angular momentum in the superconducting state, using fulleride compounds in an external magnetic field as a model system. The electron orbital angular momentum injected by an external field is transferred to the phonon subsystem via electron--phonon coupling. We show that this field-induced phonon angular momentum is significantly enhanced and undergoes a sign reversal upon entering the superconducting state. In the normal state, the dominant energy scale governing the response function is the electronic bandwidth $D$. In the superconducting state, the phonon energy scale $ω_1$ enters the denominator, leading to an enhancement of order $D/ω_1$. The observed sign change in the response can be explained by the competition between Fermi surface and Fermi volume contributions.

AI.tldr: This paper theoretically investigates phonon angular momentum in superconductors, finding that it is significantly enhanced and undergoes sign reversal when entering the superconducting state due to the competition between Fermi surface and Fermi volume contributions, with the enhancement scale of order D/ω₁.
AI.motivation: To understand the properties of phonon angular momentum in the superconducting state and how electron-phonon coupling mediates the transfer of orbital angular momentum from electrons to phonons under an external magnetic field.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis using fulleride compounds as a model system, examining the response function governing phonon angular momentum in both normal and superconducting states under an external magnetic field.
AI.result: Field-induced phonon angular momentum is significantly enhanced (by order D/ω₁) and undergoes sign reversal upon entering the superconducting state. The sign change arises from competition between Fermi surface and Fermi volume contributions.
AI.conclusion: The superconducting state fundamentally alters phonon angular momentum dynamics through a change in the dominant energy scale from electronic bandwidth D to phonon energy ω₁, leading to enhancement and sign reversal.

title: A Differentiable Programming Framework for Accurate and Stable Reduced-Order Modeling of Chaotic Flows
summary: Classical Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD)-based Galerkin projection models of chaotic flows typically require a large number of modes as well as stabilization or closure terms to achieve adequate accuracy and long-term stability. We present a novel differentiable programming framework that stabilizes low-rank POD-Galerkin models without increasing the number of modes or introducing additional closure terms, thereby delivering both high efficiency and high accuracy. Model stabilization is achieved by tuning the linear and quadratic tensors in the POD-Galerkin using differentiable programming, trained on short-term trajectory data. A key finding of this study is that a purely point-wise trajectory-based loss function yields poor long-term accuracy for chaotic systems. In contrast, a hybrid loss function that combines trajectory error with a physics-based conservation-of-energy term provides superior long-term performance. We demonstrate the approach on a chaotic lid-driven cavity flow at Re = 30,000. The stabilized ROM achieves an order-of-magnitude reduction in computational cost compared with the classical POD-Galerkin method: it remains accurate and stable with only 20 modes, whereas the classical ROM requires 80 POD modes.

AI.tldr: A differentiable programming framework stabilizes low-rank POD-Galerkin models of chaotic flows by tuning the governing tensors without adding modes or closure terms, using a hybrid loss function (trajectory error + energy conservation) to achieve long-term accuracy. Tested on chaotic lid-driven cavity flow at Re=30,000, the stabilized ROM with 20 modes outperforms classical POD-Galerkin requiring 80 modes, achieving order-of-magnitude computational cost reduction.
AI.motivation: Classical POD-Galerkin models of chaotic flows need many modes and stabilization/closure terms for accuracy and stability, which increases computational cost. The authors aim to develop a method that stabilizes low-rank ROMs without increasing mode count or adding closure terms, balancing efficiency and accuracy.
AI.method: A differentiable programming framework that tunes the linear and quadratic tensors of the POD-Galerkin model using gradient-based optimization, trained on short-term trajectory data. The loss function is hybrid: it combines point-wise trajectory error with a physics-based conservation-of-energy term to improve long-term performance.
AI.result: The stabilized ROM with only 20 modes achieves accuracy and long-term stability comparable to classical POD-Galerkin with 80 modes on a chaotic lid-driven cavity flow at Re=30,000, yielding an order-of-magnitude reduction in computational cost. Additionally, purely trajectory-based loss leads to poor long-term accuracy for chaotic systems, while the hybrid loss with energy conservation is superior.
AI.conclusion: Differentiable programming can effectively stabilize low-rank POD-Galerkin models of chaotic flows, eliminating the need for additional modes or closure terms. The hybrid physics-informed loss function is critical for long-term predictive performance in chaotic dynamical systems.

title: A High-Contrast Bragg Atom Interferometer for Testing Continuous Spontaneous Localization
summary: The continuous spontaneous localization (CSL) model is one of the most promising approaches to address the wave function collapse problem in the measurement process of standard quantum mechanics. In this work, the effect of the CSL model on a Bragg atom interferometer was investigated. A Bragg interferometer achieving high fringe contrast of 99$\%$ has been demonstrated, maintaining this performance level at interrogation time up to $T=60~\mathrm{ms}$. The primary factors responsible for fringe contrast loss in the atom interferometer were systematically analyzed and corrected. This improvement established a new upper limit of $λ_{\rm CSL}=1.27\times10^{-5}~\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ at $r_C=10^{-5}~\mathrm{m}$ for the CSL collapse rate, representing approximately 4 times enhancement over previous atom-interferometric constraints.

AI.tldr: Using a high-contrast (99%) Bragg atom interferometer with up to 60 ms interrogation time, this work establishes a new upper limit of λ_CSL = 1.27×10⁻⁵ s⁻¹ at r_C = 10⁻⁵ m for the CSL collapse rate, improving previous atom-interferometric constraints by approximately 4 times.
AI.motivation: To address the wave function collapse problem in quantum measurement by testing the continuous spontaneous localization (CSL) model, one of the most promising collapse models.
AI.method: A Bragg atom interferometer with 99% fringe contrast and interrogation times up to 60 ms was used. Systematic factors responsible for fringe contrast loss were analyzed and corrected to improve sensitivity.
AI.result: A new upper limit of λ_CSL = 1.27×10⁻⁵ s⁻¹ at r_C = 10⁻⁵ m was established, representing an approximately 4-fold improvement over previous atom-interferometric constraints.
AI.conclusion: The CSL collapse rate is constrained more tightly via improved atom interferometry techniques, demonstrating the utility of Bragg interferometers for testing collapse models.

title: Geometric Protection of Bipartite Entanglement in Hopf-Linked Quantum Rings
summary: We determine the bipartite entanglement bounds of two interacting electrons in deeply interlocked Hopf-linked quantum rings via exact diagonalization of the unexpanded 3D Coulomb interaction. This identifies an exact continuous spatial symmetry that geometrically isolates the positive-parity Bell state, preventing classical interaction-driven localization. A non-coplanar geometric tilt ($α> 0$) is essential to lift the exchange degeneracy and maintain this maximally entangled manifold as a state of frozen entanglement. However, a higher-order Schrieffer-Wolff transformation demonstrates this geometric protection is fundamentally bounded; uncancelled inter-orbital momentum transitions inevitably induce dynamical parity mixing. This defines a critical interaction threshold ($λ_{crit}$) for irreversible entanglement collapse. Our analysis shows that the resulting bounding conditions reveal scaling limitations in mesoscopic semiconductor architectures, dictating the necessity of synthetic macroscopic platforms to achieve robust topological protection.

AI.tldr: Two interacting electrons in Hopf-linked quantum rings show that geometric tilt protects a Bell state, but higher-order interactions cause unavoidable parity mixing beyond a critical threshold, limiting scalability in semiconductor systems.
AI.motivation: To determine the fundamental bounds on bipartite entanglement in geometrically intertwined quantum rings, and understand whether topological protection of Bell states is sustainable against higher-order interaction effects.
AI.method: Exact diagonalization of the full 3D Coulomb interaction (unexpanded) combined with a higher-order Schrieffer-Wolff transformation to analyze parity mixing and entanglement collapse.
AI.result: A critical interaction threshold λ_crit exists beyond which irreversible entanglement collapse occurs due to dynamical parity mixing from uncancelled inter-orbital momentum transitions.
AI.conclusion: Geometric protection of entanglement is fundamentally bounded; semiconductor architectures face scaling limitations, necessitating synthetic macroscopic platforms for robust topological protection.

title: Hydrodynamic Cooperons in Electron Fluids: Schwinger--Keldysh Derivation and Quantum Corrections to Magnetoresistance
summary: We develop a Schwinger--Keldysh effective theory for quantum-interference corrections in a two-dimensional electron system in the hydrodynamic regime. Starting from the clean hydrodynamic fixed point, we introduce a minimal random-friction disorder model that generates a finite momentum-relaxation time within the self-consistent Born approximation. The disorder-averaged theory then allows us to construct a hydrodynamic Cooperon and to compute the associated self-energy corrections to the collective modes. Conservation laws protect the density and momentum sectors, so that the leading quantum-coherence correction is forced into the spin-two stress sector. The associated stress self-energy renormalizes the shear viscosity and modifies both the Gurzhi response and its low-field magnetohydrodynamic signatures.

AI.tldr: Develops a Schwinger-Keldysh effective theory for quantum-interference corrections in 2D electron hydrodynamics, finding that conservation laws force quantum corrections into the spin-two stress sector, renormalizing shear viscosity and modifying Gurzhi response and magnetohydrodynamic signatures.
AI.motivation: To develop a theoretical framework for understanding quantum-interference (weak-localization) corrections in two-dimensional electron systems within the hydrodynamic regime, where electron-electron collisions dominate over disorder scattering.
AI.method: Starting from a clean hydrodynamic fixed point, introduces a minimal random-friction disorder model with finite momentum-relaxation time in self-consistent Born approximation. Constructs a hydrodynamic Cooperon and computes self-energy corrections to collective modes using Schwinger-Keldysh effective theory.
AI.result: Conservation laws protect density and momentum sectors, forcing the leading quantum-coherence correction into the spin-two stress sector. The stress self-energy renormalizes the shear viscosity and modifies both the Gurzhi response and low-field magnetohydrodynamic signatures.
AI.conclusion: Quantum-interference corrections in hydrodynamic 2D electron systems manifest primarily in the stress sector, providing observable signatures in shear viscosity, Gurzhi effect, and magnetohydrodynamic transport.

title: Quantum statistical mechanics: Gauge invariance, operator shifting, hyperdensity functionals, and nonequilibrium sum rules
summary: We provide an extended acount of the recent statistical mechanical theory of gauge invariance against operator shifting in quantum many-body systems (arXiv:2509.20494). The gauge transformation is enacted by a shifting superoperator that displaces the fundamental position and momentum degrees of freedom. The shifting superoperator constitutes a map between Hilbert space operators and it features Lie algebra commutator structure. Averages of general observables remain invariant under the shifting both in and out of thermal equilibrium, as well as in groundstates. The gauge invariance induces exact sum rules that interconnect global observables and associated locally resolved correlation functions. In particular we describe the resulting one-body force, hyperforce, product, and two-body sum rules. We relate the shifting superoperator to a previously formulated quantum canonical transformation and present the generalization of quantum shifting to multi-component systems. The gauge theory respects fundamental fermionic and bosonic particle properties, as we demonstrate by proving the compatibility of operator shifting and exchange symmetry. We formulate the quantum version of hyperdensity functional theory to provide formal access to hyperforces as well as to general averaged quantum observables via universal density functionals. For time-dependent situations, we describe quantum dynamical gauge invariance and prove exact dynamical sum rules for nonequilibrium situations, as generated by Hamiltonian time dependence. We argue for the fundamental status of statistical mechanical gauge invariance based on the compliance of the underlying geometry with canonical quantization according to Dirac's correspondence principle. Analogies and differences of the quantum mechanical sum rules with their classical counterparts remain indicative of the respective levels of description.

AI.tldr: This paper extends a statistical mechanical gauge theory where a shifting superoperator displaces position and momentum degrees of freedom, leaving observables invariant in and out of equilibrium. It derives exact sum rules (one-body force, hyperforce, product, two-body), relates to quantum canonical transformations, generalizes to multi-component systems, proves compatibility with exchange symmetry, formulates quantum hyperdensity functional theory, and establishes dynamical gauge invariance with exact nonequilibrium sum rules.
AI.motivation: To provide a comprehensive account of gauge invariance against operator shifting in quantum many-body systems, establishing its fundamental status via Dirac's correspondence principle and deriving exact sum rules that interconnect global observables and locally resolved correlation functions.
AI.method: A shifting superoperator that enacts gauge transformations on Hilbert space operators with Lie algebra commutator structure; extension to multi-component systems; compatibility proofs for fermionic/bosonic exchange symmetry; formulation of quantum hyperdensity functional theory; derivation of equilibrium and nonequilibrium dynamical sum rules.
AI.result: Gauge invariance holds for general observables in thermal equilibrium, out-of-equilibrium, and ground states. Exact one-body force, hyperforce, product, and two-body sum rules are derived. The theory is compatible with quantum statistics and generalizes to multi-component systems. Dynamical gauge invariance and exact nonequilibrium sum rules are proven.
AI.conclusion: Statistical mechanical gauge invariance has fundamental status, grounded in the geometry of canonical quantization. Quantum sum rules show both analogies and differences with classical counterparts, reflecting distinct levels of description.

title: Resilience of the physicochemical properties of graphene-based materials for applications in harsh radiation environments
comment: 17 pages, submitted to Diamond & Related Materials
summary: The development of radiation-tolerant materials capable of maintaining structural, electrical, and thermal stability in extreme, radiation-rich environments remains a critical challenge in materials science. In this work, the effects of 60 MeV 35Cl ion irradiation on highly oriented pyrolytic graphite (HOPG) and multilayer reduced graphene oxide (ML-rGO) were investigated. The samples were exposed to fluences of 5.11 x 10^9 and 1.3 x 10^10 ions/cm^2 and characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD), Raman spectroscopy, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), atomic force microscopy (AFM), and electrical transport measurements. The results show that the irradiation response is strongly influenced by the initial structural organization of the material. In HOPG, ion exposure leads to a progressive loss of crystalline order, evidenced by XRD peak broadening and an increase in the Raman ID/IG ratio, accompanied by a reduction in electrical transport performance. In contrast, ML-rGO exhibits distinct behavior at higher fluences, suggesting partial structural reorganization. The appearance of more defined graphitic features in XRD and Raman analyses, along with changes in surface morphology and electrical response, suggests the formation of more ordered sp2 domains. These findings indicate that irradiation effects vary with the initial degree of order, providing useful insights for selecting carbon-based materials for devices operating under severe radiation conditions.

AI.tldr: This study investigates the effects of 60 MeV 35Cl ion irradiation on HOPG and ML-rGO, finding that HOPG suffers progressive crystalline degradation while ML-rGO shows signs of partial structural reorganization and increased sp2 ordering at higher fluences.
AI.motivation: To understand how different initial structural organizations in carbon-based materials respond to extreme radiation environments, addressing the need for radiation-tolerant materials for devices operating under severe conditions.
AI.method: HOPG and ML-rGO samples were irradiated with 60 MeV 35Cl ions at fluences of 5.11×10^9 and 1.3×10^10 ions/cm^2, then characterized using XRD, Raman spectroscopy, SEM, AFM, and electrical transport measurements.
AI.result: HOPG shows progressive loss of crystallinity (XRD peak broadening, increased ID/IG ratio, reduced electrical performance). ML-rGO exhibits distinct behavior at higher fluences, with more defined graphitic features in XRD/Raman, morphological changes, and indications of sp2 domain formation.
AI.conclusion: Irradiation effects depend on the initial degree of structural order; less-ordered ML-rGO can undergo partial reorganization, offering insights for selecting carbon-based materials in radiation-rich environments.

title: Analytic first order nonadiabatic coupling matrix elements of spin-adapted open-shell time-dependent density functional theory
summary: While spin-adapted time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT) approaches significantly improve the excitation energies and gradients of open-shell molecules, the effect of spin-adaptation on nonadiabatic coupling matrix elements (NACMEs) remains unknown for spin-conserving excitations. In this article, we report the derivation, implementation and benchmark studies of the ground state-excited state and excited state-excited state NACMEs of our spin-adapted TDDFT method, X-TDDFT. Similar to the X-TDDFT analytic gradients, X-TDDFT NACMEs can be easily implemented on top of an existing U-TDDFT NACME implementation taking into account the restricted open-shell Kohn-Sham (ROKS) reference and the implicit involvement of doubly excited determinants, with acceptable computational overhead. Benchmark calculations reveal that X-TDDFT reduces the error of U-TDDFT NACMEs by 1/3-2/3 (referenced against high-level multireference NACMEs), which leads to large corrections of internal conversion rates (up to two orders of magnitude). In particular, for copper(II) porphyrin, X-TDDFT leads to qualitative revisions of the dominant excited state relaxation pathway, as well as the substituent effects of the internal conversion rates, suggesting that the error of U-TDDFT NACMEs is not only large but also unsystematic. It is therefore expected that X-TDDFT NACMEs will prove useful in the photophysics/photochemistry studies of open-shell systems such as radicals and transition metal complexes.

AI.tldr: This paper derives, implements, and benchmarks spin-adapted (X-TDDFT) nonadiabatic coupling matrix elements, showing they reduce U-TDDFT errors by 1/3-2/3 and qualitatively correct internal conversion pathways in open-shell systems like copper(II) porphyrin.
AI.motivation: While spin-adapted TDDFT improves excitation energies and gradients of open-shell molecules, the effect of spin-adaptation on NACMEs for spin-conserving excitations was previously unknown.
AI.method: Derivation and implementation of ground state-excited state and excited state-excited state NACMEs for X-TDDFT, built upon existing U-TDDFT NACME implementations with ROKS reference and implicit doubly excited determinants.
AI.result: X-TDDFT reduces U-TDDFT NACME errors by 1/3-2/3 (referenced against multireference methods), leading to corrections of internal conversion rates up to two orders of magnitude. For copper(II) porphyrin, it qualitatively revises the dominant relaxation pathway and substituent effects.
AI.conclusion: X-TDDFT NACMEs are expected to be useful for photophysics/photochemistry studies of open-shell systems such as radicals and transition metal complexes, as U-TDDFT errors are both large and unsystematic.

title: Impact of Stoichiometry of MoSi Thin Films for Enhanced Sensitivity of Superconducting Nanowire Single-Photon Detectors
summary: We report on the impact of the stoichiometry of superconducting MoSi thin films on the performance of superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors (SNSPDs). Specifically, we investigate the relation between the film parameters critical temperature Tc , sheet resistance Rs and superconductor thickness d and observe a universal scaling behavior. To benchmark the performance of SNSPDs fabricated from films having different stoichiometry, we measure the bias dependent count rate curves, while the detector is illuminated with wavelengths between 780 nm and 1550 nm. The detector performance as a function photon energy for different nanowire widths reveals a linear relation between the detection current and the photon energy. Furthermore, we determine the interfacial thermal boundary conductance $β$ between the superconducting thin film and the substrate, by measuring the return current of the SNSPD and find an increase of $β$ with increasing Mo concentration. The highest sensitivity amongst all compared devices is achieved for Mo$_{0.53}$Si$_{0.47}$, with low Tc (4.1 K) and high Rs (397$Ω$/sq) at a film thickness of 5.4 nm.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how MoSi thin film stoichiometry affects SNSPD performance, finding a universal scaling between Tc, Rs, and thickness, and identifying Mo0.53Si0.47 as the optimal composition with highest sensitivity.
AI.motivation: To understand the impact of MoSi stoichiometry on superconducting film parameters and SNSPD device performance, and to establish structure-property-performance relationships for optimizing detector design.
AI.method: Systematically varied MoSi stoichiometry, measured Tc, Rs, and thickness to observe scaling behavior; characterized SNSPD count rate under 780-1550 nm illumination; measured interfacial thermal boundary conductance via return current analysis.
AI.result: Linear relation between detection current and photon energy across nanowire widths; interfacial thermal boundary conductance increases with Mo concentration; Mo0.53Si0.47 (Tc=4.1 K, Rs=397 Ω/sq, d=5.4 nm) yields best sensitivity.
AI.conclusion: Film stoichiometry critically controls SNSPD performance through Tc and Rs; the optimal composition balances low Tc and high Rs for maximum sensitivity.

title: Conditions for domain-free negative capacitance
summary: While negative capacitance has been demonstrated in ferroelectric-dielectric heterostructures in the form of capacitance enhancement, all experimental evidence, to date, suggests the existence of domains therein. Here, we address the question: what are the conditions to achieve ideal, domain-free negative capacitance in ferroelectric-dielectric heterostructures? Our main claim is that for given thicknesses of the ferroelectric and the dielectric layers, there is a critical value of domain wall energy parameter -- above which the system would be stabilized in an ideal and robust domain-free negative capacitance state and would be robust against domain formation. Our analyses suggest that to achieve ideal negative capacitance, efforts should lie in understanding the means to control the domain wall energy on all fronts, both theory and experiments via high throughput design, discovery, and engineering of ferroelectrics.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies that a critical domain wall energy parameter exists in ferroelectric-dielectric heterostructures, above which ideal, domain-free negative capacitance can be achieved and stabilized, shifting the focus from polarization screening to domain wall engineering.
AI.motivation: To determine the conditions under which ideal, domain-free negative capacitance can be achieved in ferroelectric-dielectric heterostructures, given that all prior experimental evidence shows domain formation rather than the idealized single-domain state.
AI.method: Analytical modeling of ferroelectric-dielectric heterostructures with given layer thicknesses, identifying a critical domain wall energy threshold that separates domain-free (ideal negative capacitance) from domain-forming states.
AI.result: There exists a critical value of domain wall energy parameter; above this threshold, the system is stabilized in a robust, domain-free negative capacitance state that resists domain formation.
AI.conclusion: Achieving ideal negative capacitance requires controlling domain wall energy through high-throughput design, discovery, and engineering of ferroelectrics, both theoretically and experimentally.

title: Local Surrogates for Harmonic Vibrational Entropy in Multilattices
summary: Harmonic vibrational entropy is a key finite-temperature contribution to defect thermodynamics, but direct evaluation by dense Hessian diagonalization scales cubically with atom count and is too costly for supercell convergence, migration-path sampling, and high-throughput defect studies. We develop local surrogate models for harmonic entropy in multilattices, including semiconductors, ordered alloys, and multispecies crystals with multi-atom bases and internal degrees of freedom. Unlike Bravais lattices, multilattices contain internal-shift degrees of freedom and optical phonon modes coupled to acoustic strain; entropy models must therefore resolve sublattice and species labels. For finite-range or screened atomistic models, we prove sublattice-resolved locality and cutoff-error estimates that justify replacing the global entropy calculation by a local, symmetry-respecting regression problem with controlled truncation error. This turns vibrational entropy from a global spectral calculation into a reusable local site model with linear evaluation cost at fixed cutoff. Numerical tests confirm the predicted locality behavior and show that sublattice/species-resolved surrogates achieve accurate regression, transfer across supercell sizes, and linear-scaling evaluation on Stillinger--Weber Si and CdTe benchmarks. The resulting method enables repeated harmonic-entropy evaluations in multispecies defect calculations while retaining explicit stability, truncation, and surrogate-error controls.

AI.tldr: The paper develops local surrogate models for harmonic vibrational entropy in multilattices (semiconductors, ordered alloys) to replace costly global Hessian diagonalization, achieving linear-scaling evaluation with provable locality guarantees and accurate regression on Si and CdTe benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Direct harmonic entropy evaluation via Hessian diagonalization scales cubically with atom count, making it prohibitive for supercell convergence, migration-path sampling, and high-throughput defect studies in multispecies crystals.
AI.method: Local surrogate models for harmonic entropy are developed for multilattices with internal degrees of freedom. The authors prove sublattice-resolved locality and cutoff-error estimates, reformulating the global spectral calculation into a local, symmetry-respecting regression problem with controlled truncation error and linear evaluation cost.
AI.result: Numerical tests on Stillinger-Weber Si and CdTe confirm predicted locality behavior, accurate sublattice/species-resolved regression, transferability across supercell sizes, and linear-scaling evaluation.
AI.conclusion: The method enables repeated harmonic-entropy evaluations in multispecies defect calculations with explicit stability, truncation, and surrogate-error controls, making vibrational entropy tractable for large-scale defect thermodynamics.

title: Experimental and theoretical studies of hyperfine structures in $^{21}$Na
summary: We measured the hyperfine structure constants, $A(3s^2S_{1/2})$ and $A(3p^2P_{1/2})$, of the neutron-deficient isotope $^{21}\text{Na}$ using CLaSsy, a setup dedicated to collinear laser spectroscopy at RAON. The hyperfine structure constants of $^{21}\text{Na}$ were measured to be $103.6(10)_{\mathrm{stat}}(9)_{\mathrm{syst}}$ MHz for $A(3p^2P_{1/2})$ and $954.9(11)_{\mathrm{stat}}(25)_{\mathrm{syst}}$ MHz for $A(3s^2S_{1/2})$. A systematic comparison with the state-of-the-art ab-initio relativistic coupled cluster calculations shows the role of higher-order correlation effects such as triple excitations in $^{21}$Na. Furthermore, the measurement demonstrates a capability of the CLaSsy setup to conduct collinear laser spectroscopy experiments with a radioactive beam.

AI.tldr: This paper reports the measurement of hyperfine structure constants A(3s²S₁/₂) and A(3p²P₁/₂) for the neutron-deficient isotope ²¹Na using the CLaSsy collinear laser spectroscopy setup at RAON, achieving high-precision values that enable comparison with ab-initio relativistic coupled cluster calculations and demonstrate the setup's capability for radioactive beam experiments.
AI.motivation: To measure hyperfine structure constants of the neutron-deficient isotope ²¹Na and validate the CLaSsy setup for collinear laser spectroscopy with radioactive beams at RAON.
AI.method: Collinear laser spectroscopy using the CLaSsy setup at RAON, with statistical and systematic uncertainty quantification.
AI.result: A(3p²P₁/₂) = 103.6(10)ₛₜₐₜ(9)ₛᵧₛₜ MHz; A(3s²S₁/₂) = 954.9(11)ₛₜₐₜ(25)ₛᵧₛₜ MHz.
AI.conclusion: The measurements reveal the importance of higher-order correlation effects (triple excitations) in ²¹Na and demonstrate that CLaSsy is capable of conducting collinear laser spectroscopy with radioactive beams.

title: Terahertz spin-current transparency through rough interfaces
summary: Spin transport across interfaces is critical for spintronic devices, yet remains difficult to probe on ultrafast timescales. We use terahertz emission spectroscopy on Co|Pt heterostructures whose interface roughness is tuned through the thickness of an underlying Au buffer layer, while leaving other growth parameters unchanged. From the measured THz electric field, we extract the interface spin-current transparency ts after correcting for the changes in sample impedance and optical absorption of the stack. Surprisingly, we find that ts decreases by only approximately 30% as the interface root-mean-square roughness and the lateral grain size both increase by a factor of three, with no measurable change in the THz spectrum. These results demonstrate that interfacial spin transport is relatively robust against morphological variations on ultrafast timescales, establishing terahertz emission spectroscopy as a reliable probe of spin dynamics across imperfect interfaces.

AI.tldr: Using terahertz emission spectroscopy on Co|Pt heterostructures with controlled interface roughness, the study finds that interface spin-current transparency decreases only ~30% even when roughness and grain size triple, showing ultrafast interfacial spin transport is robust against morphological variations.
AI.motivation: Spin transport across interfaces is critical for spintronic devices, yet remains difficult to probe on ultrafast timescales.
AI.method: Terahertz emission spectroscopy on Co|Pt heterostructures whose interface roughness is tuned through the thickness of an underlying Au buffer layer, while leaving other growth parameters unchanged.
AI.result: Interface spin-current transparency ts decreases by only ~30% as interface RMS roughness and lateral grain size both increase by a factor of three, with no measurable change in the THz spectrum.
AI.conclusion: Interfacial spin transport is relatively robust against morphological variations on ultrafast timescales, establishing terahertz emission spectroscopy as a reliable probe of spin dynamics across imperfect interfaces.

title: GPU-accelerated finite-temperature Lanczos method for spin Hamiltonians
summary: We present a GPU implementation of the finite-temperature Lanczos method (FTLM) for Heisenberg spin Hamiltonians that targets workstation hardware rather than distributed-memory clusters. The Hamiltonian action is evaluated matrix-free in a row-wise gather formulation. We introduce and compare two state-to-index strategies: a compressed lookup table (CLT), which reduces lookup memory by a factor of 16 relative to a full table while retaining a fixed, branch-light access pattern, and a GPU-adapted combinatorial-ranking scheme that removes the lookup table altogether. Numerical tests against FP64 CPU references show that FP32 GPU arithmetic changes heat capacities and magnetic susceptibilities by amounts several orders of magnitude below the stochastic uncertainty of the FTLM trace estimator at typical sample sizes. Benchmarks show speedups of up to about one order of magnitude over optimized multicore CPU calculations and enable Hilbert-space sectors of dimension ~10^8 on a single workstation GPU. The MATLAB/CUDA implementation, including example input files and benchmark scripts, is openly available at https://github.com/ghasdeke/ftlm-gpu (archived at DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.20378647) under the Apache-2.0 license.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a GPU-accelerated finite-temperature Lanczos method (FTLM) for Heisenberg spin Hamiltonians, using matrix-free evaluation and two state-to-index mapping strategies (compressed lookup table and combinatorial ranking). FP32 precision is sufficient, and the implementation achieves ~10x speedup over multicore CPUs, handling sectors up to ~10^8 on a single workstation GPU. Code is open-source under Apache-2.0.
AI.motivation: To accelerate the finite-temperature Lanczos method for Heisenberg spin Hamiltonians on GPU hardware accessible to individual workstations, rather than requiring distributed-memory clusters.
AI.method: Matrix-free Hamiltonian action using a row-wise gather formulation; two state-to-index mapping strategies: compressed lookup table (CLT, 16× memory reduction) and a GPU-adapted combinatorial ranking scheme (table-free). FP32 arithmetic used with verification against FP64 CPU references.
AI.result: FP32 GPU errors in heat capacity and magnetic susceptibility are orders of magnitude below FTLM stochastic uncertainty. Speedups of ~10× over optimized multicore CPUs. Hilbert-space sectors up to ~10^8 on a single workstation GPU.
AI.conclusion: GPU-accelerated FTLM is viable on workstation hardware, offering significant speedups without sacrificing accuracy, and the implementation is openly available.

title: Spatiotemporal Structures of Parametrically Driven Nonlinear Lattices
summary: We theoretically investigate the effects of parametric driving on the one-dimensional Frenkel-Kontorova model, a nonlinear many-body lattice system. It is numerically found that a parametric vibration induces spatiotemporal ordering characterized by the subharmonic frequency $ω_{\mathrm{ex}}/2$ and wavenumber $k$ which takes nontrivial values depending on the vibration strength $P_{\mathrm{ac}}$ and frequency $ω_{\mathrm{ex}}$. With increasing $P_{\mathrm{ac}}$, $k$ gradually increases and discontinuously jumps up to $k=π$. Based on an extended linear stability analysis, we show that the former $k$ resonance (the latter $π$ resonance) corresponds to the unstable (stable) mode and that the $k$ resonance is made possible by the interplay between the parametric amplification and the collective fluctuation developing through the nonlinear effect.

AI.tldr: This paper theoretically studies parametric driving effects on the 1D Frenkel-Kontorova model, finding that parametric vibration induces spatiotemporal ordering with subharmonic frequency ω_ex/2 and wavenumber k that varies with driving strength. As Pac increases, k rises gradually then jumps discontinuously to π, corresponding to unstable/stable modes via extended linear stability analysis.
AI.motivation: To understand how parametric driving influences nonlinear many-body lattice systems, specifically the Frenkel-Kontorova model, and to reveal the mechanisms behind parametric resonance and spatiotemporal ordering.
AI.method: Numerical simulation of the parametrically driven 1D Frenkel-Kontorova model combined with an extended linear stability analysis.
AI.result: Parametric vibration induces spatiotemporal ordering with subharmonic frequency ω_ex/2 and wavenumber k that increases with driving strength Pac and discontinuously jumps to k=π. The k resonance corresponds to an unstable mode while the π resonance corresponds to a stable mode.
AI.conclusion: The k resonance arises from the interplay between parametric amplification and collective fluctuations developing through nonlinear effects.

title: Finite Temperature Stacking Fault Stability in Random and Locally Ordered CoCrNi beyond the Harmonic Approximation
summary: Previous density functional theory (DFT) calculations for random solid solution (RSS) CoCrNi predict negative intrinsic stacking-fault energy (ISFE) at 0 K, contrary to experimental observations of finite stacking-fault widths. Two explanations have been proposed: finite-temperature stabilization of the RSS state, suggested by harmonic approximations showing increasing ISFE with temperature, and local chemical order (LCO), which shifts the ISFE to positive values at 0 K. Here, we compute temperature-dependent generalized stacking-fault free energies for RSS and LCO CoCrNi using a near-quantum-accuracy machine learning interatomic potential and the fully anharmonic projected average force integrator. Unlike harmonic approximations, our anharmonic calculations show that the RSS ISFE decreases with temperature and remains negative, indicating that RSS stacking faults are not thermally stabilized at elevated temperatures. By contrast, LCO maintains positive ISFE over 0-1000 K. Molecular dynamics simulations further confirm unbounded dislocation dissociation in RSS CoCrNi but finite stacking-fault widths in the LCO state.
