AI.tldr: Anharmonic calculations show that random solid solution (RSS) CoCrNi has negative intrinsic stacking-fault energy (ISFE) that decreases with temperature, while local chemical order (LCO) maintains positive ISFE over 0-1000 K, explaining finite stacking-fault widths only in the LCO state.
AI.motivation: To resolve the discrepancy between DFT-predicted negative ISFE in RSS CoCrNi at 0 K and experimental observations of finite stacking-fault widths, by testing whether finite-temperature stabilization or local chemical order explains the positive ISFE.
AI.method: Used a near-quantum-accuracy machine learning interatomic potential and the fully anharmonic projected average force integrator to compute temperature-dependent generalized stacking-fault free energies for both RSS and LCO CoCrNi.
AI.result: Anharmonic calculations show RSS ISFE decreases with temperature and remains negative; LCO maintains positive ISFE from 0-1000 K. MD simulations confirm unbounded dislocation dissociation in RSS but finite stacking-fault widths in LCO.
AI.conclusion: Local chemical order, not thermal stabilization, is responsible for the experimentally observed finite stacking-fault widths in CoCrNi; harmonic approximations overestimate thermal stabilization effects.

title: Electronic Structure in a Phase Space, non-Born-Oppenheimer Framework: Geometric Forces and Moody-Shapere-Wilzcek Revisited
summary: We revisit the three-body problem in quantum mechanics in two and three dimensions, generating both exact eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the Hamiltonian and a series of approximate solutions as calculated with a variety of different schemes to separate heavy ("nuclear") and light ("electronic") particles. We show that, with minimal extra cost, one can go beyond the Born-Oppenheimer approximation by performing electronic structure calculations parameterized by both the nuclear position (${\mathbf X})$ and the nuclear momentum ($\mathbf{P}$), a so-called phase space theory of electronic structure. In particular, we demonstrate that such phase space electronic structure calculations correctly incorporate the non-inertial Coriolis and centrifugal forces felt by electrons in a moving nuclear frame, thus leading to far more accurate eigenenergies and electronic angular momenta than has been possible before. We also demonstrate that our approach naturally incorporates and generalizes the Moody-Shapere-Wilczek magnetic monopole for the non-abelian Berry curvature (now allowing for vibrational motion rather than a diatomic of fixed length). We argue that the resulting approach should be extremely useful for propagating dynamics where angular momentum flows between nuclei and electrons; in particular, if extended to include spin degrees of freedom, the present approach will offer a practical means to study chiral induced spin selectivity through the lens of chiral phonons and coupled nuclear-electronic motion.

AI.tldr: The paper revisits the three-body quantum problem, developing a phase-space electronic structure theory that goes beyond the Born-Oppenheimer approximation by parameterizing the Hamiltonian with both nuclear position and momentum. This correctly incorporates Coriolis and centrifugal forces, yielding more accurate eigenenergies and angular momenta, and generalizes the Moody-Shapere-Wilczek magnetic monopole to non-adiabatic Berry curvature with vibrational motion.
AI.motivation: To overcome limitations of the Born-Oppenheimer approximation by developing a phase-space theory of electronic structure that accounts for non-inertial forces (Coriolis and centrifugal) experienced by electrons in moving nuclear frames, enabling more accurate eigenenergies and angular momenta.
AI.method: The authors revisit the three-body problem in 2D and 3D quantum mechanics, generating exact eigenvalues/eigenvectors and comparing approximate solutions from various schemes. They develop a phase-space electronic structure approach parameterized by both nuclear position (X) and nuclear momentum (P), which goes beyond the standard Born-Oppenheimer framework at minimal extra cost.
AI.result: The phase-space method correctly incorporates Coriolis and centrifugal forces, producing far more accurate eigenenergies and electronic angular momenta than conventional approaches. It naturally generalizes the Moody-Shapere-Wilczek magnetic monopole description of non-abelian Berry curvature to include vibrational motion (beyond fixed-length diatomics).
AI.conclusion: The approach is promising for propagating dynamics involving angular momentum flow between nuclei and electrons. If extended to spin degrees of freedom, it could enable practical study of chiral induced spin selectivity via chiral phonons and coupled nuclear-electronic motion.

title: Electride States and Superconductivity in Dense Potassium Carbides
summary: Carbon possesses remarkable physicochemical properties, enabling main group metals to react with it under high pressure and produce superconducting compounds. However, the research on high-pressure potassium carbides remains still unsystematic and inadequate. Using first-principles calculations and state-of-the-art swarm intelligence structure prediction techniques, we comprehensively explore the binary novel potassium-carbon system and characterize their structural, electronic, and superconducting properties under compression. Calculations of electron-phonon coupling show that monoclinic K7C (space group C2/m) with high K concentration is a zero-dimensional electride superconductor with a transition temperature Tc of 0.6 K at 25 GPa. By contrast, the Tc of orthorhombic KC with symmetry Imma increases upon decompression owing to the phonon softening of both acoustic and optical branches. Impressively, Imma KC reaches a maximum Tc of 21.4 K at 25 GPa, which is highly desirable for low-pressure metallic carbide superconductors. This work provides valuable insights into K-C compounds and broadens the diversity of metal carbide superconductors.

AI.tldr: First-principles calculations and swarm intelligence structure prediction reveal two novel K-C superconductors under high pressure: a zero-dimensional electride K7C (Tc=0.6 K at 25 GPa) and a high-Tc orthorhombic KC (Tc=21.4 K at 25 GPa), broadening the diversity of metal carbide superconductors.
AI.motivation: Research on high-pressure potassium carbides remains unsystematic and inadequate, despite carbon's remarkable properties enabling main group metals to form superconducting compounds under high pressure.
AI.method: First-principles calculations combined with state-of-the-art swarm intelligence structure prediction techniques to explore the K-C system under compression, analyzing structural, electronic, and superconducting properties.
AI.result: Discovered two superconducting phases: monoclinic K7C (C2/m) with Tc=0.6 K at 25 GPa as a zero-dimensional electride, and orthorhombic KC (Imma) with Tc reaching 21.4 K at 25 GPa via phonon softening upon decompression.
AI.conclusion: This work provides valuable insights into K-C compounds and broadens the diversity of metal carbide superconductors, with Imma KC being highly desirable as a low-pressure metallic carbide superconductor.

title: Orbital and Spin-Orbit Torque Interplay in Ta/W-based Magnetic Tunnel Junctions with Vertical Non-local Switching
summary: Spin-orbit torque (SOT) enables ultra-fast, energy-efficient magnetization switching, making it a promising mechanism for introducing MRAMs for cache memory applications. However, current SOT-MRAM devices face write efficiency limitations, with charge-to-spin conversion ($ξ_{DL}$) reaching $\sim$ 45\%, far below the projected $\sim$ 80\% needed to comply with the current delivery of advanced transistor nodes. Recent advances in orbital current physics, evidenced in a wide class of materials, offer a path to enhance $ξ_{DL}$. Here, we study the Ta(3-30 nm)\slash W(1-4 nm) system, revealing a large additional spin-orbit torque contribution arising from Ta, a four-fold increase compared to the spin Hall effect in Ta alone, attributed to the orbital Hall contribution. This system exhibits larger $ξ_{DL}$ than W-based SOT systems with more robust perpendicular magnetic anisotropy and compatibility with 400$^\circ$C annealing. Leveraging these advantages, we integrate the Ta/W system into 3-terminal SOT-MTJ devices, showing a level of performance similar to that of W-based systems. Our results show that orbital physics can be easily integrated into SOT-MTJ systems, offering a viable strategy to enhance SOT-MRAM efficiency. In addition, we propose and demonstrate a proof-of-concept for vertical non-local switching of SOT-MTJ using orbital torques, simplifying bottom-pinned SOT-MRAM fabrication.

AI.tldr: The study demonstrates that incorporating orbital Hall contributions from a Ta/W bilayer system significantly enhances spin-orbit torque efficiency (four-fold increase over Ta alone), achieving performance comparable to W-based systems while offering better perpendicular magnetic anisotropy and thermal stability, thereby providing a viable path to improve SOT-MRAM for cache memory applications.
AI.motivation: Current SOT-MRAM devices suffer from insufficient charge-to-spin conversion efficiency (ξ_DL ~45%), far below the ~80% required for compatibility with advanced transistor nodes, limiting their adoption in cache memory applications.
AI.method: The authors study a Ta(3-30 nm)/W(1-4 nm) bilayer system, leveraging orbital Hall physics to enhance SOT. They integrate this system into 3-terminal SOT-MTJ devices and also propose a proof-of-concept for vertical non-local switching using orbital torques.
AI.result: The Ta/W system exhibits a four-fold increase in SOT compared to the spin Hall effect in Ta alone, attributed to orbital Hall contributions. It shows larger ξ_DL than W-based SOT systems, with more robust perpendicular magnetic anisotropy and compatibility with 400°C annealing, achieving performance similar to W-based systems in 3-terminal SOT-MTJ devices.
AI.conclusion: Orbital physics can be readily integrated into SOT-MTJ systems, offering a viable strategy to enhance SOT-MRAM efficiency. The demonstration of vertical non-local switching using orbital torques also simplifies bottom-pinned SOT-MRAM fabrication.

title: Direct Dispersion-Curve Engineering of Phononic Crystal Defect Modes for Prescribed Frequencies via Topology Optimization
summary: Phononic crystals enable precise manipulation of elastic wave propagation through engineered bandgaps; however, designing defect states within these bandgaps for frequency-selective applications remains a significant challenge. Existing design approaches, including prior optimization formulations, struggle to systematically resolve the competing objectives of attracting desired defect modes to target frequencies while simultaneously repelling unwanted modes from the bandgap region. This inability to suppress competing modes often results in spurious, undesired in-gap resonant modes, thereby limiting design purity. This paper presents a novel two-stage topology optimization framework that addresses this challenge through an innovative multi-objective formulation based on a selection function with Gaussian weighting. In the first stage, the unit cell topology is optimized to create a wide bandgap around a target frequency. In the second stage, a supercell containing a defect is optimized using a specially designed objective function that dynamically balances mode attraction and repulsion via a selection function $S(ω)$ with adaptive $σ$ parameters. This selection mechanism enables the optimizer to automatically identify and selectively attract the most suitable defect mode while repelling competing modes from the bandgap region, eliminating the need for manual mode tracking. Numerical examples demonstrate that the proposed framework successfully generates phononic crystals featuring engineered defect states that yield precisely positioned localized resonant modes at prescribed frequencies within wide bandgaps, with potential applications in frequency-selective filters and elastic wave manipulation devices.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a two-stage topology optimization framework for designing phononic crystals with defect states that achieve precise frequency-selective localized resonant modes, using a multi-objective selection function with Gaussian weighting to automatically attract desired modes while repelling unwanted ones.
AI.motivation: Existing design approaches struggle to systematically balance attracting desired defect modes to target frequencies while repelling unwanted modes from the bandgap region, often resulting in spurious in-gap resonant modes that limit design purity.
AI.method: A two-stage topology optimization framework: Stage 1 optimizes unit cell topology to create a wide bandgap around a target frequency; Stage 2 optimizes a defect-containing supercell using a multi-objective formulation based on a selection function S(ω) with adaptive σ parameters, dynamically balancing mode attraction and repulsion without manual mode tracking.
AI.result: The framework successfully generates phononic crystals with engineered defect states that produce precisely positioned localized resonant modes at prescribed frequencies within wide bandgaps.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method effectively eliminates spurious in-gap modes and enables automated design of frequency-selective phononic crystal devices, with potential applications in filters and elastic wave manipulation.

title: Active learning of collinear magnetic Moment Tensor Potentials using the spin-MLIP package from soft-constrained spin-polarized DFT calculations: a case study of Fe-Pd
summary: Explicit incorporation of magnetic degrees of freedom in machine-learning interatomic potentials (magnetic MLIPs) plays a crucial role in the correct description of magnetic materials and their properties. An important ingredient for fitting of magnetic MLIPs is spin-polarized density functional theory (DFT) calculations with non-equilibrium magnetic moments, i.e. DFT calculations with constraints on magnetic moments. In this study, we present a workflow for active learning of magnetic Moment Tensor Potential (mMTP) during molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. Magnetic MTP and its active learning algorithm were implemented in the open-source spin-MLIP code, DFT soft-constrained spin-polarized calculations were performed with the VASP code, and MD simulations were conducted in the open-source LAMMPS code. We test our workflow on the Fe-Pd crystal. The dependencies of magnetization and density of states (DOSs) on the volume of a supercell (or, pressure) are in good agreement with those calculated with DFT. Furthermore, the calculated DOSs correspond to the experimental ones.

AI.tldr: A workflow for active learning of magnetic Moment Tensor Potential (mMTP) during MD simulations is presented, integrating spin-MLIP, VASP, and LAMMPS codes, and validated on Fe-Pd crystal showing good agreement with DFT and experimental results.
AI.motivation: Magnetic MLIPs are crucial for describing magnetic materials but require spin-polarized DFT calculations with constrained magnetic moments; an efficient active learning workflow is needed to generate training data on-the-fly during MD simulations.
AI.method: Developed an active learning workflow for mMTP during MD simulations, implemented in spin-MLIP code, using DFT soft-constrained spin-polarized calculations (VASP) and MD simulations (LAMMPS), tested on Fe-Pd crystal.
AI.result: Magnetization and DOS dependencies on supercell volume/pressure from mMTP match DFT calculations well; calculated DOSs correspond to experimental data.
AI.conclusion: The active learning workflow for mMTP successfully reproduces DFT-level accuracy for magnetic properties of Fe-Pd, validating its utility for magnetic materials simulation.

title: Orbital Magnetization from Uniform and Periodic Magnetic Fields
summary: Magnetization is thermodynamically defined as the derivative of the grand potential with respect to a uniform magnetic field. However, a uniform magnetic field makes the kinetic momentum operators noncommuting and Landau-quantizes the electron motion. This changes the zero-field momentum-space to Landau-levels and raises a fundamental question: how can the thermodynamic response to a uniform field be reproduced by a linear-response calculation carried out in the momentum space of the zero-field problem? We address this question analytically in a quantum Hall ferromagnet that allows the orbital magnetization $M$ to be computed in a closed form. We first compute $M$ from the local Hartree--Fock projector response to a periodic magnetic field with zero net flux. We then compute $M$ from the derivative of the grand potential with respect to a uniform magnetic field along the Středa line. The two approaches give the same result, even though the first keeps the Hilbert space fixed while the second changes the Landau-level degeneracy. Their agreement suggests that we should view orbital magnetization as the energy associated with the spectral flow that gives rise to the Středa formula. Our work provides a tutorial introduction to orbital magnetization and its relation to the Středa formula.

AI.tldr: This paper resolves the apparent paradox between thermodynamic and linear-response calculations of orbital magnetization in a quantum Hall ferromagnet, showing that both approaches yield identical results and suggesting orbital magnetization should be understood as energy associated with spectral flow in the Středa formula.
AI.motivation: To address the fundamental question of how thermodynamic response to a uniform magnetic field can be reproduced by linear-response calculations carried out in the zero-field momentum space, given that a uniform field Landau-quantizes electron motion and makes kinetic momentum operators noncommuting.
AI.method: Analytical calculations in a quantum Hall ferromagnet: (1) Computing orbital magnetization from local Hartree-Fock projector response to a periodic magnetic field with zero net flux; (2) Computing orbital magnetization from the derivative of the grand potential with respect to a uniform magnetic field along the Středa line, demonstrating agreement between the two approaches.
AI.result: The two approaches yield the same orbital magnetization, even though the first keeps the Hilbert space fixed while the second changes Landau-level degeneracy. This agreement validates the equivalence of thermodynamic and linear-response formulations.
AI.conclusion: Orbital magnetization should be viewed as the energy associated with the spectral flow that gives rise to the Středa formula. The work serves as a tutorial introduction to orbital magnetization and its relation to the Středa formula.

title: Nematic Phase Transitions in Multilayer Graphene Systems
summary: Recent experiments on graphene multilayers under displacement field have demonstrated a wide variety of electronically ordered phases, including valley and/or spin polarized phases as well as potentially unconventional superconducting phases. In addition, quantum oscillation measurements in Bernal bilayer graphene and rhombohedral trilayer graphene showed the presence of electronic nematic states. Here, we investigate the emergence of nematic order in these systems, with emphasis on Bernal bilayer graphene, within a self-consistent Hartree--Fock framework, using a realistic band structure with trigonal warping and a dual-gate screened Coulomb interaction. We compute the phase diagram as carrier density and displacement field are varied, and find a sequence of isospin (spin and valley) polarized states consistent with experiment, including partially polarized phases with a large Fermi pockets for isospin-majority carriers and smaller Fermi pockets for isospin-minority carriers. Within these partially isospin polarized states, we identify regions with three $C_3$-symmetric pockets for the minority carriers and regions with only one or two such pockets, implying that the system develops a spontaneous nematic order that breaks $C_3$ symmetry. We find numerically that nematicity emerges near the boundary between fully and partially polarized phases and is controlled by the strength of the screened interaction. We analytically derive a criterion for the nematic order, which agrees with our numerical results.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates nematic order in Bernal bilayer graphene within a Hartree-Fock framework, finding that nematicity emerges near the boundary between fully and partially isospin polarized phases, driven by screened Coulomb interactions, and confirms this with an analytical criterion.
AI.motivation: Recent experiments on graphene multilayers revealed various electronically ordered phases (valley/spin polarized, unconventional superconducting, and nematic states), motivating a theoretical investigation of nematic order emergence in Bernal bilayer graphene and rhombohedral trilayer graphene.
AI.method: Self-consistent Hartree-Fock framework with a realistic band structure including trigonal warping and dual-gate screened Coulomb interaction, computing phase diagrams as carrier density and displacement field vary.
AI.result: Found a sequence of isospin polarized states consistent with experiment; identified regions with three C3-symmetric pockets for minority carriers vs. one or two pockets, indicating spontaneous nematic order breaking C3 symmetry; nematicity emerges near the boundary between fully and partially polarized phases, controlled by screened interaction strength.
AI.conclusion: Nematic order in Bernal bilayer graphene arises near the phase boundary between fully and partially isospin polarized states, driven by screened Coulomb interactions; an analytical criterion derived agrees with numerical findings.

title: Long-range deformations in Gaussian States
summary: Imaginary-time evolution by a local Hamiltonian cannot induce a phase transition in one dimension, but longer-range interactions may subvert such constraints. Starting from the ground state of the Kitaev Majorana chain, we modify the wave function by an imaginary-time evolution generated by a quadratic Hamiltonian with power-law couplings that enhance pairing correlations, typically of the form $1/r^α$, where $r$ is the distance between two sites. As the state remains Gaussian, entanglement and correlation functions can be computed analytically. We find that the decay exponent $α$ controls three distinct infrared regimes: for $α>1$, the deformation produces only smooth crossovers at finite deformation strength, while the topological regime is reached only asymptotically as the deformation strength tends to infinity. At $α=1$, the deformation induces an immediate flow to the topological phase: an infinitesimal deformation strength drives the system to a topological regime, and in a particular case, an emergent Kramers-Wannier symmetry enforces Ising-like scaling at long distances. For $α<1$, the deformed state shows the same critical-like behavior for all non-zero deformation strength. We observe that even with arbitrarily long-range interactions, these models do not display a sharp phase transition at non-zero deformation strength.

AI.tldr: This paper studies imaginary-time evolution of the Kitaev Majorana chain with power-law interactions (1/r^α). It finds three regimes: smooth crossover for α>1, topological phase transition at α=1, and critical-like behavior for α<1, but no sharp phase transition at finite deformation strength.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether longer-range interactions in imaginary-time evolution can induce phase transitions in one dimension, where local Hamiltonians cannot, and to understand the role of the decay exponent α in controlling entanglement and correlation properties.
AI.method: Starting from the ground state of the Kitaev Majorana chain, the wave function is modified by imaginary-time evolution generated by a quadratic Hamiltonian with power-law pairing couplings ∝1/r^α. The state remains Gaussian, enabling analytical computation of entanglement and correlation functions.
AI.result: Three distinct infrared regimes are identified based on α: (1) α>1: smooth crossovers at finite deformation strength, topological regime only asymptotically; (2) α=1: immediate flow to topological phase, with emergent Kramers-Wannier symmetry and Ising-like scaling; (3) α<1: critical-like behavior for all non-zero deformation strength. No sharp phase transition occurs at non-zero deformation strength even with arbitrarily long-range interactions.
AI.conclusion: Even with arbitrarily long-range interactions, these models do not exhibit a sharp phase transition at non-zero deformation strength. The decay exponent α=1 is identified as a marginal case that induces an immediate topological phase transition.

title: Dyck language and fermionic second quantization: I. Theory
summary: This paper proposes a novel framework connecting fermionic second quantization and Dyck languages. By defining translations of creation and annihilation operators using bracket alphabets, the study establishes nullity criteria for expectation values of chains of second quantization operators. Those translations are designed to reveal sufficient conditions for the nullity of the expectation values relatively to one-determinant states or to the physical vacuum. The nullity criteria are purely syntactic, and simply reduce to the inspection of sequences of opening and closing brackets. Moreover, numbers and transformations in Dyck languages can be imported in the context of fermionic second quantization. One of these numbers, the depth, originally absent from second quantization, can be used to introduce more nullity criteria.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a framework linking fermionic second quantization with Dyck languages, using bracket-based translations of creation/annihilation operators to derive purely syntactic nullity criteria for expectation values based on bracket sequence inspection, and imports Dyck language concepts like depth for additional criteria.
AI.motivation: To establish purely syntactic (rather than algebraic) nullity criteria for expectation values of fermionic second quantization operator chains, and to bridge formal language theory (Dyck languages) with quantum many-body physics.
AI.method: Translating creation/annihilation operators using bracket alphabets; analyzing nullity of expectation values (relative to one-determinant states or physical vacuum) via syntactic inspection of opening/closing bracket sequences; importing Dyck language concepts (e.g., depth) into the fermionic context.
AI.result: Sufficient conditions for nullity of expectation values are purely syntactic, reducible to bracket sequence inspection; Dyck language numbers and transformations (e.g., depth) yield additional nullity criteria.
AI.conclusion: The connection between fermionic second quantization and Dyck languages enables novel, syntax-driven nullity criteria and enriches second quantization with formal language theory tools.

title: Neural Autoregressive Control Variates for the Quantum Monte Carlo Sign Problem
summary: We train a pair of autoregressive models to construct zero-mean control variates to mitigate the sign problem in quantum Monte Carlo simulations. The two autoregressive networks are confined to the positive- and negative-sign sectors with strictly disjoint support, and each is exactly normalized over its sector. Their difference is therefore structurally zero-mean, providing an unbiased auxiliary observable whose correlation with the sign estimator controls the variance reduction. We implement the method within the stochastic series expansion framework, which we extend to frustrated lattices by developing an incremental loop-topology update. Sign-ergodic sampling is achieved through a twist channel, which is the unique sign-changing mechanism on non-bipartite lattices. We implement the control variates as autoregressive transformers with an end-of-sequence parity mask that enforces exact sign-sector resolution, while the incremental loop-count change and cumulative frustration parity are incorporated as topological features. On the triangular-lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnet, we benchmark the method in the small-$N$ limit. The control variate reduces the standard error of the average sign by up to an order of magnitude and that of the energy estimator by a factor of three to five, remaining effective even when the average sign drops below $10^{-3}$. This work lays out the framework and provides a proof-of-principle demonstration that autoregressive control variates can effectively mitigate the sign problem. Scaling to larger systems with physics-informed architectures is the subject of future work.

AI.tldr: Autoregressive neural networks are used to construct zero-mean control variates that reduce the sign problem in quantum Monte Carlo simulations, achieving up to an order of magnitude reduction in standard error on the triangular-lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnet benchmark.
AI.motivation: The sign problem in quantum Monte Carlo simulations causes exponential variance that severely limits the study of frustrated quantum systems. Existing variance reduction techniques are insufficient when the average sign becomes extremely small.
AI.method: Two autoregressive transformer models are trained to operate on strictly disjoint positive- and negative-sign sectors with exact normalization. Their difference yields a zero-mean control variate. The method is implemented within stochastic series expansion with an incremental loop-topology update for frustrated lattices. Sign-ergodic sampling uses a twist channel, and an end-of-sequence parity mask enforces exact sign-sector resolution.
AI.result: On the triangular-lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnet (small-N limit), the control variate reduces the standard error of the average sign by up to an order of magnitude and the energy estimator error by a factor of 3-5, remaining effective even when the average sign drops below 10⁻³.
AI.conclusion: Autoregressive control variates can effectively mitigate the sign problem in quantum Monte Carlo, providing a proof-of-principle demonstration. Scaling to larger systems with physics-informed architectures is identified as future work.

title: Anomaly-Induced Hybrid Bulk Electromagnetic Mode in Weyl Semimetals
summary: Collective modes provide direct fingerprints of quantum matter. We predict a previously unidentified hybrid bulk electromagnetic mode in Weyl semimetals arising from the interplay between the chiral anomaly and the orientation of its associated chiral magnetic response relative to the direction of the wave-vector. When the anomaly-induced chiral magnetic current has a component along the propagation direction, oscillations of valley imbalance hybridize with plasmonic charge oscillations, producing a linearly dispersing mode that undergoes avoided crossing with the bulk plasmon, producing a hybrid bulk excitation absent in ordinary metals. The hybrid mode provides a direct signature of Weyl semimetals and a probe of the chiral anomaly and its associated chiral magnetic effect, with observable features in electron energy-loss spectroscopy. Studying this interplay can uncover various optical and electronic properties of Weyl semimetals.

AI.tldr: The paper predicts a new hybrid bulk electromagnetic mode in Weyl semimetals, arising from the coupling between the chiral anomaly and the chiral magnetic response orientation relative to wave propagation. This mode hybridizes valley imbalance oscillations with plasmonic charge oscillations, producing a linearly dispersing mode that undergoes avoided crossing with the bulk plasmon, observable via electron energy-loss spectroscopy.
AI.motivation: To identify a direct electromagnetic fingerprint of Weyl semimetals that arises from the chiral anomaly and its associated chiral magnetic effect, providing both a signature of Weyl physics and a probe of anomalous transport properties.
AI.method: Theoretical prediction and analytical derivation of the hybrid bulk electromagnetic mode by analyzing the interplay between the chiral anomaly-induced chiral magnetic current and the direction of wave-vector propagation relative to the current orientation.
AI.result: Discovery of a linearly dispersing hybrid mode arising from oscillations of valley imbalance hybridizing with plasmonic charge oscillations, which undergoes avoided crossing with the bulk plasmon, forming a hybrid bulk excitation absent in ordinary metals.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid mode serves as a direct signature of Weyl semimetals and a probe of the chiral anomaly and chiral magnetic effect, with observable features in electron energy-loss spectroscopy, offering insights into the optical and electronic properties of Weyl semimetals.

title: Ground state correlations in the one-dimensional Fermi one-component plasma
summary: Structural and dynamic correlations in the ground state of the one-dimensional Fermi one-component plasma are studied by Quantum Monte Carlo simulations. Results are presented for the pair correlation function, static structure factor, the one-particle density matrix and the momentum distribution, for the cases of full, partial and no polarization. Evidence is reported of density correlations slowly decaying with distance, with the concurrent emergence of quasi-crystalline order even in the weakly correlated regime. Effects of quantum statistics in the momentum distribution are discussed.

AI.tldr: Quantum Monte Carlo simulations of the 1D Fermi one-component plasma reveal slowly decaying density correlations and quasi-crystalline order across polarization regimes, with analysis of quantum statistics effects on momentum distribution.
AI.motivation: To investigate structural and dynamic correlations in the ground state of the one-dimensional Fermi one-component plasma across different polarization conditions.
AI.method: Quantum Monte Carlo simulations are used to compute pair correlation function, static structure factor, one-particle density matrix, and momentum distribution for full, partial, and no polarization cases.
AI.result: Evidence of slowly decaying density correlations with distance and emergence of quasi-crystalline order even in the weakly correlated regime. Quantum statistics effects are observed in the momentum distribution.
AI.conclusion: The 1D Fermi one-component plasma exhibits quasi-crystalline order and long-range density correlations beyond the weakly correlated regime, with polarization-dependent quantum statistical effects.

title: A tridiagonal matrix-valued process with stochastic resetting for arbitrary Dyson index $β>0$
summary: We introduce a symmetric tridiagonal matrix-valued process ($β$-TMP) $H(t)$ whose diagonal entries $H_{k,k}(t)$ evolve independently via an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process starting at the origin and the off-diagonal entries $H_{k,k+1}(t)$ evolve independently via the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross process, starting at the origin and with parameters that depend on the row index $k$. We show that the joint distribution of the entries of the matrix can be computed exactly at all times and moreover, the joint distribution of its $N$ real eigenvalues can be computed exactly at all times too. We then subject this time-evolving matrix-valued process to stochastic resetting with rate $r$ in two different settings: (i) simultaneous resetting of the matrix entries to the origin with rate $r$ ($β$-SRTMP process) and (ii) independent resetting of the matrix entries to the origin with rate $r$ ($β$-IRTMP process). We show that the joint distribution of the eigenvalues of the $β$-SRTMP process at long times can be computed analytically and it coincides with the joint distribution of the positions of the resetting Dyson Brownian motion in its stationary state for arbitrary $β>0$. For the $β$-IRTMP stationary ensemble, computing analytically the joint distribution of eigenvalues or even the average density of eigenvalues is difficult. However, generating the stationary $β$-IRTMP ensemble numerically is relatively straightforward and we compare its numerical average eigenvalue density to the corresponding analytical results for the $β$-SRTMP stationary ensemble with same parameter values, showing that they are quite different from each other. Finally, we provide a simple and concrete application of this tridiagonal matrix-valued process in computing the annealed partition function of a disordered quantum tight-binding Hamiltonian on a one-dimensional lattice.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a symmetric tridiagonal matrix-valued process (β-TMP) with Ornstein-Uhlenbeck diagonals and Cox-Ingersoll-Ross off-diagonals. It studies two stochastic resetting variants (simultaneous β-SRTMP and independent β-IRTMP), derives exact joint eigenvalue distributions for β-SRTMP, compares stationary ensembles numerically, and applies the process to compute the annealed partition function of a disordered quantum tight-binding Hamiltonian.
AI.motivation: To construct exactly solvable time-dependent random matrix ensembles with stochastic resetting, and to connect such processes to the statistical physics of disordered quantum systems.
AI.method: Define a tridiagonal matrix process β-TMP with independent OU-process diagonal entries and CIR-process off-diagonal entries. Introduce two resetting protocols: simultaneous (β-SRTMP) and independent (β-IRTMP). Derive exact joint eigenvalue distributions analytically for β-SRTMP; generate β-IRTMP numerically and compare eigenvalue densities.
AI.result: The joint eigenvalue distribution of β-SRTMP at long times equals that of resetting Dyson Brownian motion stationary state for any β>0. The β-IRTMP stationary ensemble is not analytically tractable but numerically simulated, revealing significant differences from the β-SRTMP ensemble. The process is applied to compute the annealed partition function of a disordered tight-binding Hamiltonian.
AI.conclusion: The β-TMP framework provides exactly solvable models of random matrices under resetting, with the simultaneous-resetting case yielding analytical stationary eigenvalue statistics, while the independent-resetting case remains analytically challenging but numerically accessible. The work bridges random matrix theory, stochastic resetting, and disordered quantum systems.

title: Structural Alter-Phononics: Sublattice-Momentum Locking in Spinless Lattice Dynamics
summary: The discovery of altermagnetism has shown that crystal symmetry can generate momentum-dependent internal polarization without net magnetization. Whether an analogous form of symmetry-organized momentum-space order can exist for spinless lattice vibrations remains unresolved. Here we identify a structural mechanism for $alter$-$phononics$, in which phonon eigenmodes formed from structurally equivalent sublattices acquire momentum-dependent sublattice polarization and frequency splitting in nonmagnetic crystals. The central quantity is the sublattice-resolved dynamical asymmetry $Δ(\mathbf q)=D_{AA}(\mathbf q)-D_{BB}(\mathbf q)$, which controls the associated eigenvector polarization. We show that this effect requires an alter-generator that maps equivalent sublattices onto one another while rotating the wave vector, together with the absence of inversion exchange and little-group sublattice-exchange constraints that would otherwise enforce sublattice equipartition. These symmetry rules generate nematic $d$-wave, tetragonal $d/g$-wave, and tripartite six-lobe phonon textures. First-principles calculations demonstrate the mechanism in representative nonmagnetic crystals and show how a symmetry-preserving structural distortion can unlock a hidden $d_{x^2-y^2}$-type texture by removing glide-induced equipartition traps while retaining the screw-axis alter-generator. We further show that the eigenvector texture is inherited by sublattice-projected electron-phonon coupling and anharmonic response functions. Our results establish structural alter-phononics as a spinless counterpart to altermagnetic momentum-space order and provide experimentally testable signatures in finite-$\mathbf q$ phonon spectra and displacement patterns.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a structural mechanism for "alter-phononics," where phonon eigenmodes in nonmagnetic crystals acquire momentum-dependent sublattice polarization and frequency splitting—a spinless counterpart to altermagnetism—governed by sublattice-resolved dynamical asymmetry and specific symmetry rules, with first-principles validation and experimentally testable signatures.
AI.motivation: To determine whether a symmetry-organized momentum-space order analogous to altermagnetism (momentum-dependent polarization without net magnetization) can exist for spinless lattice vibrations (phonons) in nonmagnetic crystals.
AI.method: The authors identify a structural mechanism where phonon eigenmodes from structurally equivalent sublattices develop momentum-dependent sublattice polarization and frequency splitting. They define the sublattice-resolved dynamical asymmetry Δ(q) = D_AA(q) - D_BB(q), derive symmetry rules requiring an alter-generator (mapping equivalent sublattices while rotating wave vector) and the absence of inversion exchange and little-group sublattice-exchange constraints, and perform first-principles calculations on representative nonmagnetic crystals.
AI.result: The symmetry rules generate nematic d-wave, tetragonal d/g-wave, and tripartite six-lobe phonon textures. First-principles calculations show how a symmetry-preserving structural distortion can unlock a hidden d_{x²-y²}-type texture by removing glide-induced equipartition traps while retaining the screw-axis alter-generator. The eigenvector texture is inherited by sublattice-projected electron-phonon coupling and anharmonic response functions.
AI.conclusion: Structural alter-phononics is established as a spinless counterpart to altermagnetic momentum-space order, providing experimentally testable signatures in finite-q phonon spectra and displacement patterns.

title: Dyck language and fermionic second quantization: II. Applications
summary: In this work, we establish a direct connection between supplemented Dyck language and the signed expectation value of chains of second quantization operators relatively to the physical vacuum and relatively to a one-determinant state. Inspired by the fact that Dyck language provides an example of the emergence of the Catalan numbers in linguistic framework analysis, we show that these numbers are central when numbering the terms remaining when eliminating vanishing contributions detected by our application of Dyck language to fermionic second quantization. From the translation of creation and annihilation operator - or of pairs of operators - into a bracket alphabet, we derive simple and intuitive sufficient conditions for the nullity of expectation values that does not require an explicit application of Wick's theorem. This is done here with respect to the physical vacuum or relatively to a one-determinant state. We also extend this translation into a diagrammatic framework that allows a visual determination of the signature of fully contracted terms, reproducing the results of Wick's theorem. This approach has been extended to the case of (nested) commutators of pairs of fermionic second quantization including at least one excitation or deexcitation operator. Our results have been implemented in a software, MobiDyck, whose source code is freely available on the web. The algorithmic approach inspired by our work on Dyck language is detailed in this paper. Finally, a comparison of our diagrammatic approach with Goldstone diagrams is provided and closes the article.

AI.tldr: This paper connects supplemented Dyck language to expectation values of fermionic second quantization operators, using Catalan numbers to count non-vanishing terms, deriving nullity conditions without Wick's theorem, extending to diagrammatic frameworks and commutators, and implementing results in the open-source software MobiDyck.
AI.motivation: To establish a direct connection between Dyck language (and Catalan numbers) and fermionic second quantization, providing intuitive sufficient conditions for nullity of expectation values without explicit Wick's theorem application.
AI.method: Translating creation/annihilation operators into a bracket alphabet; applying Dyck language structure to identify vanishing contributions; extending to diagrammatic framework for visual determination of signatures; generalizing to nested commutators with excitation/deexcitation operators; implementing algorithmic approach in MobiDyck software.
AI.result: Catalan numbers emerge as central for counting non-vanishing terms; simple sufficient conditions for nullity of expectation values derived; diagrammatic framework reproduces Wick's theorem results; extension to commutators of fermionic operators achieved; software implementation provided.
AI.conclusion: Dyck language provides a powerful linguistic and diagrammatic framework for analyzing fermionic second quantization, with practical software implementation and comparison to Goldstone diagrams.

title: Defect engineering of ultrathin gallium nitride via electric fields for advanced electronic, magnetic, and gas sensing applications
summary: Scaling wide-band-gap semiconductors to the ultrathin limit offers a transformative pathway for power electronics, with gallium nitride (GaN) representing a cornerstone material in this class. However, the operational resilience and functional tunability of its two-dimensional form (g-GaN) remain underexplored. This work shifts the focus from idealized systems to the complex materials behavior under realistic conditions, investigating how the synergistic effects of point vacancy defects, strain, and external electric fields govern its electronic, magnetic, and sensing landscapes. We demonstrate that these factors are not merely perturbations but are fundamental to modulating the material response. Our first-principles calculations suggest g-GaN maintains electronic stability under intense electric fields; notably, gallium vacancies are predicted to further extend the theoretical stability limit. While in-plane tension preserves the band gap evolution under an electric field, in-plane compression facilitates low-field metallization. Using nitrogen monoxide (NO) adsorption as a prototype, we find that the interaction is defect-modulated and potentially tunable by electric fields. Analysis of adsorption energetics and diffusion barriers suggests the gallium vacancy may act as a thermodynamic trap for NO. Targeted hybrid-functional (HSE06) validation confirms the reliability of observed adsorption trends and theoretical metallization thresholds, while revealing that precise electronic-exchange treatment is critical for capturing the magnetic ground state of nitrogen vacancies. By systematically examining the geometry, energetics, band structure, density of states, magnetic response, and charge transfer, this study clarifies the interplay between defects and external electric fields, providing insights into theoretical upper bounds for property tuning and semiconductor device engineering.

AI.tldr: This study uses first-principles calculations to investigate how point vacancy defects, strain, and external electric fields synergistically govern the electronic, magnetic, and sensing properties of two-dimensional gallium nitride (g-GaN), revealing that these factors are fundamental modulators of material behavior with implications for power electronics and device engineering.
AI.motivation: The operational resilience and functional tunability of two-dimensional gallium nitride (g-GaN) remain underexplored, despite GaN being a cornerstone wide-band-gap semiconductor for power electronics. This work shifts focus from idealized systems to complex materials behavior under realistic conditions.
AI.method: First-principles calculations with hybrid-functional (HSE06) validation, systematically examining geometry, energetics, band structure, density of states, magnetic response, and charge transfer under synergistic effects of point vacancies, strain, and external electric fields.
AI.result: g-GaN maintains electronic stability under intense electric fields; gallium vacancies extend the theoretical stability limit. In-plane tension preserves band gap evolution under electric fields, while compression enables low-field metallization. NO adsorption is defect-modulated and tunable by electric fields; gallium vacancies act as thermodynamic traps for NO.
AI.conclusion: The interplay between defects and external electric fields is fundamental to modulating g-GaN's properties, providing insights into theoretical upper bounds for property tuning and semiconductor device engineering.

title: Quantum Geometric Origin of Hall Viscosity and Nonlocal Hall Conductivity in Lattice Bands
summary: We show that Hall viscosity in lattice bands is governed by a band-projected electric quadrupole encoded within the quantum geometry: Berry curvature sets the projected-coordinate algebra, while the quantum metric determines the quadrupolar spread of a wave packet. The same structure enters the quadratic wave-vector coefficient of the nonlocal Hall conductivity, yielding a lattice viscosity-conductivity relation. In ideal bands, the deviation from the Landau-level form is quantified by Berry curvature fluctuations. Our results establish the nonlocal Hall response as an electrical signature of the quantum geometry underlying Hall viscosity and as a transport diagnostic of geometric idealness.

AI.tldr: Hall viscosity in lattice bands is governed by a band-projected electric quadrupole linked to quantum geometry—Berry curvature sets the projected-coordinate algebra and quantum metric determines wave-packet quadrupolar spread—leading to a lattice viscosity-conductivity relation where nonlocal Hall response serves as an electrical probe of quantum geometry and geometric idealness.
AI.motivation: To establish the connection between Hall viscosity and quantum geometry in lattice bands, and to identify an electrical (nonlocal Hall) signature that can experimentally probe the geometric properties underlying Hall viscosity.
AI.method: Theoretical derivation linking Hall viscosity to band-projected electric quadrupole, Berry curvature, and quantum metric; analysis of quadratic wave-vector coefficient of nonlocal Hall conductivity to establish a lattice viscosity-conductivity relation; quantification of deviation from Landau-level form via Berry curvature fluctuations in ideal bands.
AI.result: Hall viscosity in lattice bands is governed by band-projected electric quadrupole from quantum geometry; Berry curvature determines projected-coordinate algebra; quantum metric determines quadrupolar spread; nonlocal Hall conductivity's quadratic coefficient yields a viscosity-conductivity relation; deviation from Landau-level form in ideal bands is quantified by Berry curvature fluctuations.
AI.conclusion: Nonlocal Hall response is an electrical signature of the quantum geometry underlying Hall viscosity and serves as a transport diagnostic of geometric idealness.

title: Surface d-orbital order in intermetallic compound
summary: Orbital order describes a quantum state where occupied orbitals line up in a periodic pattern. While orbital physics plays a fundamental and universal role in strongly correlated electron systems, the existence and particularly the band structure fingerprint of orbital order remain a long-standing mystery. Here, we report the discovery of rare earth 5d-orbital order developed by the surface states of intermetallic compound Tb2CoAl4Ge2. Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy reveals characteristic nematic features like Fermi surface deformation and band split. These experimental observations can be described by a ferro-orbital order term in the mean-field Hamiltonian. The structural and magnetic origin of such order is excluded by systematic high-resolution neutron powder diffraction and scanning tunnelling microscopy measurements. Our results provide strong evidence for a pure surface orbital order scenario avoiding complications from structural distortion as in colossal magnetoresistance manganites, magnetic order as in iron-based superconductors, and charge transfer p-orbital order in cuprates.

AI.tldr: This paper reports the discovery of rare earth 5d-orbital order in the surface states of Tb₂CoAl₄Ge₂, confirmed via ARPES showing nematic features, with structural and magnetic origins excluded by neutron diffraction and STM, providing evidence for a pure surface orbital order.
AI.motivation: Orbital order remains a long-standing mystery in strongly correlated electron systems; the existence and band structure fingerprint of orbital order have not been clearly established.
AI.method: Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) was used to observe nematic features; neutron powder diffraction and scanning tunnelling microscopy (STM) ruled out structural and magnetic origins; a ferro-orbital order term in the mean-field Hamiltonian described the observations.
AI.result: Discovery of rare earth 5d-orbital order in Tb₂CoAl₄Ge₂ surface states, with characteristic nematic features such as Fermi surface deformation and band splitting observed via ARPES.
AI.conclusion: The observed orbital order is purely electronic in nature (surface orbital order), avoiding complications from structural distortion (as in manganites), magnetic order (as in iron-based superconductors), or charge transfer p-orbital order (as in cuprates).

title: Subdiffusion equation with Cattaneo effect
summary: The ordinary subdiffusion equation, with a fractional time derivative of at most first order, describes a process in which the propagation velocity of diffusing molecules is unlimited. To avoid this non-physical property different forms of the Cattaneo subdiffusion equation have been proposed. We define the Cattaneo effect as a delay of the ordinary subdiffusion flux activation by a random time. By incorporating this effect into the flux equation we get a Cattaneo--type subdiffusion equation (CTSE). We consider a subdiffusion process in which the Cattaneo effect is generated by the time-delay probability distribution controlled by the Mittag-Leffler function. Then, CTSE differs from the ordinary subdiffusion equation by a term with a fractional time derivative, whose order can be independent of the subdiffusion exponent. The influence of the Cattaneo effect on the solutions to the CTSE is discussed. We show that the process described by CTSE is subdiffusion in the entire time domain even though the temporal evolution of the mean square displacement of diffusing particle in the short-time limit is typical for superdiffusion. The delay in the flux activation in the subdiffusion equation should also cause a flux delay in a boundary condition. As an example, we study subdiffusion with the Cattaneo effect in a system with a partially absorbing wall at which the Robin boundary condition is assumed. We also propose a method for experimentally identifying the Cattaneo effect in a subdiffusive system.

AI.tldr: This paper defines the Cattaneo effect as a random time delay in subdiffusion flux activation, leading to a Cattaneo-type subdiffusion equation (CTSE) with a fractional time derivative of independent order. The resulting process exhibits subdiffusion overall but superdiffusion-like short-time MSD, and the effect is studied under Robin boundary conditions with proposed experimental identification.
AI.motivation: The ordinary subdiffusion equation has unlimited propagation velocity (non-physical). Different Cattaneo-type subdiffusion equations have been proposed to address this, but the authors aim to provide a unified probabilistic interpretation via a random time delay in flux activation.
AI.method: The Cattaneo effect is modeled as a random delay in subdiffusion flux activation, governed by a Mittag-Leffler time-delay distribution. This yields a Cattaneo-type subdiffusion equation (CTSE) containing an additional fractional time derivative term with an order independent of the subdiffusion exponent. The analysis includes solutions, mean square displacement behavior, and boundary condition modifications (Robin type).
AI.result: The CTSE describes subdiffusion across the entire time domain, yet the short-time MSD exhibits superdiffusion-like scaling. The additional fractional derivative order is decoupled from the subdiffusion exponent. A method for experimental identification of the Cattaneo effect is proposed, and the influence on Robin boundary conditions is analyzed.
AI.conclusion: The Cattaneo effect, defined as a random delay in flux activation, resolves the unphysical infinite propagation speed in ordinary subdiffusion. The proposed CTSE captures finite-speed effects while retaining subdiffusive behavior overall, with experimentally testable signatures.

title: Modulation of charge density waves in a twisted vortex moire superlattice
summary: Twisted moire superlattices in van-der-Waals heterostructures provide a powerful platform for engineering correlated states through moire-band reconstruction. However, whether globally coherent electronic orders can be continuously manipulated at the nanoscale remains largely unexplored. Reconstructed moire structures in small-angle and near-commensurate regime feature continuously varying local environments, offering new opportunities for nanoscale manipulation of correlated phases. Here, we report the modulation of charge density wave (CDW) states in a twisted vortex moire superlattice formed between monolayer VTe2 and superconducting NbSe2. Scanning tunneling microscopy/spectroscopy reveals that the intrinsic long-range CDW of monolayer VTe2 is reconstructed into inequivalent local phases with distinct stability and coherence within a single moire unit cell, including suppressed CDW order and enhanced short-range CDW correlations persisting to room temperature. First-principles calculations show that the reconstructed CDW landscape originates from strong local strain variation, where compressive strain substantially stabilizes the charge order. Furthermore, the modulated CDW states exhibit competing interplay with proximity-induced superconductivity. Our results establish vortex moire superlattices as a versatile platform for nanoscale manipulation of correlated electronic orders in low-dimensional quantum materials.

AI.tldr: Twisted VTe₂/NbSe₂ moiré superlattices enable nanoscale manipulation of charge density wave states via local strain variations, producing distinct CDW phases within a single moiré unit cell, including room-temperature short-range correlations and competing interactions with proximity-induced superconductivity.
AI.motivation: To explore whether globally coherent electronic orders can be continuously manipulated at the nanoscale using twisted moiré superlattices, particularly in the small-angle and near-commensurate regime where continuously varying local environments exist.
AI.method: Scanning tunneling microscopy/spectroscopy combined with first-principles calculations on a twisted vortex moiré superlattice formed between monolayer VTe₂ and superconducting NbSe₂.
AI.result: Intrinsic long-range CDW in monolayer VTe₂ is reconstructed into inequivalent local phases within a single moiré unit cell, including suppressed CDW and enhanced short-range CDW correlations persisting to room temperature. Compressive strain stabilizes charge order, and modulated CDW competes with proximity-induced superconductivity.
AI.conclusion: Vortex moiré superlattices offer a versatile platform for nanoscale manipulation of correlated electronic orders in low-dimensional quantum materials.

title: Real-Time Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory for Pump-Probe Spectroscopies
summary: The last decade has witnessed a rapid advancement in laser technology, enabling the direct monitoring and control of electronic motion on its natural attosecond to sub-femtosecond timescales. Ultrafast processes are conventionally studied using pump-probe spectroscopic techniques, where a pump pulse drives the molecule out of equilibrium and a time-delayed probe pulse records the response of the coherent non-stationary state. Since, these processes are non-linear and non-perturbative in nature, real-time formalisms provide a suitable theoretical framework for studying ultrafast light-induced dynamics. In addition, relativistic effects can play an important role in such simulations, either because the external field lies in the XUV to soft-X-ray region targeting core-level excitations, or because the molecular system contains heavy elements. In this chapter, we provide an overview of recent developments in real-time time-dependent density functional theory for simulating pump-probe spectroscopies (namely, transient absorption and transient electronic circular dichroism) at both non-relativistic and relativistic Hamiltonian levels. In order to further interpret these spectroscopic signals, we analyze several spectroscopically relevant time-dependent sub-observables, such as induced electronic densities and induced dipole moments as well as analytical formulations of generalized non-equilibrium response functions. We provide examples to show that the framework can be used to investigate and design new light-induced phenomena that emerge only in the attosecond regime.

AI.tldr: This chapter reviews recent developments in real-time time-dependent density functional theory (RT-TDDFT) for simulating pump-probe spectroscopies (transient absorption and transient electronic circular dichroism) at both non-relativistic and relativistic levels, focusing on attosecond to sub-femtosecond light-induced dynamics. It analyzes time-dependent sub-observables and response functions to interpret and design new phenomena in the attosecond regime.
AI.motivation: Laser technology advances now enable monitoring electronic motion on attosecond timescales, requiring suitable theoretical frameworks to study ultrafast, non-linear, non-perturbative light-induced dynamics in molecular systems, especially where relativistic effects arise from XUV/soft-X-ray fields or heavy elements.
AI.method: Real-time time-dependent density functional theory (RT-TDDFT) framework is employed at both non-relativistic and relativistic Hamiltonian levels to simulate pump-probe spectroscopies (transient absorption and transient electronic circular dichroism). Analytical formulations of non-equilibrium response functions and time-dependent sub-observables (induced electronic densities, induced dipole moments) are used to interpret spectroscopic signals.
AI.result: The framework can simulate transient absorption and transient electronic circular dichroism spectra, analyze induced electronic densities and dipole moments, and formulate generalized non-equilibrium response functions, enabling investigation of attosecond-regime light-induced phenomena.
AI.conclusion: The RT-TDDFT framework is suitable for studying and designing new light-induced phenomena that emerge exclusively in the attosecond regime, bridging ultrafast spectroscopy with ab initio electronic structure theory.

title: Molecular Dynamics Study of Defect Evolution Mechanisms in 3C-SiC for Quantum Technologies
summary: The migration of point defects and formation of spin defects in 3C-SiC were investigated using molecular dynamics simulations, with migration barriers obtained from Nudged Elastic Band (NEB) calculations and finite temperature diffusivities evaluated using both mean square displacement (MSD) and jump frequency approaches. While both methods reproduce Arrhenius behavior, the jump frequency formulation exhibits improved statistical stability. Activation energies of 2.12~eV for carbon vacancies and 0.88~eV for carbon interstitials are obtained, consistent with literature. The resulting mobility hierarchy governs defect evolution and complex formations. Interstitial vacancy recombination competes with vacancy aggregation into divacancies, influencing the stabilization of spin active defect centers. The study also provides a consistent framework for diffusion analysis in atomistic simulations.

AI.tldr: MD simulations and NEB calculations of point defect migration in 3C-SiC show carbon vacancies (2.12 eV) and interstitials (0.88 eV) activation energies, with jump frequency method offering better statistical stability than MSD; the mobility hierarchy governs defect evolution, with I-V recombination competing with divacancy formation, impacting spin defect stabilization.
AI.motivation: To understand point defect migration and spin defect formation mechanisms in 3C-SiC, which is important for quantum applications relying on spin-active defect centers.
AI.method: Molecular dynamics simulations with NEB-derived migration barriers; finite-temperature diffusivities computed via both MSD and jump frequency approaches; Arrhenius analysis for activation energies.
AI.result: Activation energies: carbon vacancies ~2.12 eV, carbon interstitials ~0.88 eV; jump frequency method yields better statistical stability than MSD; mobility hierarchy dictates evolution of defects and complexes.
AI.conclusion: Interstitial-vacancy recombination competes with vacancy aggregation into divacancies, affecting spin defect center stabilization; the study provides a consistent atomistic diffusion analysis framework.

title: Microwave-driven Floquet-Fano interference in a ring-chord quantum dot structure for enhanced spin-caloritronic performance
summary: We investigate photon-assisted thermoelectric transport in four--quantum-dot nanostructures featuring ring and ring--chord geometries coupled to ferromagnetic leads. Focusing on the interplay between microwave-induced Floquet sidebands and geometry-driven Fano interference, we employ the nonequilibrium Green's function formalism combined with Floquet theory and a self-consistent Hartree treatment of electron-electron interactions within the linear response regime. The inclusion of a longitudinal interdot chord bridging the lead-coupled dots introduces a discrete interference pathway that competes with the continuum of ring-mediated states, giving rise to pronounced Fano resonances. Microwave irradiation dynamically reshapes these resonances through photon absorption and emission processes, enabling tunable control of electrical conductance, thermopower, and electronic thermal conductance. Quantitatively, at an intermediate temperature of $T=0.3Γ_0$ (where $Γ_0$ denotes the dot-lead coupling strength), the microwave-driven ring-chord geometry exhibits an exceptional thermoelectric figure of merit of ZT $\approx$ 12 and an optimal efficiency--power trade-off, reaching nearly $62\%$ of the Carnot efficiency with an output power of $6.24~\mathrm{fW}$. Crucially, the combination of spin-polarized injection from the leads and Zeeman splitting within the dots induces a robust spin-dependence within this Floquet--Fano interference. This cooperative interplay results in an enhanced spin Seebeck response and a maximum spin thermoelectric figure of merit of nearly $Z_sT \approx 18$. Our findings establish microwave-driven engineering of Fano interference as an effective strategy for modulating spin-caloritronic behavior in multi-quantum-dot devices.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates photon-assisted thermoelectric transport in four-quantum-dot nanostructures with ring and ring-chord geometries coupled to ferromagnetic leads, using nonequilibrium Green's function formalism with Floquet theory and Hartree treatment. The microwave-driven ring-chord geometry achieves ZT ≈ 12 and 62% of Carnot efficiency, while spin-polarized injection yields a spin figure of merit ZsT ≈ 18, demonstrating microwave engineering of Fano interference for spin-caloritronic modulation.
AI.motivation: To explore how microwave-induced Floquet sidebands and geometry-driven Fano interference can be synergistically combined to achieve tunable control of thermoelectric and spin-caloritronic transport in multi-quantum-dot nanostructures.
AI.method: Nonequilibrium Green's function formalism combined with Floquet theory and self-consistent Hartree treatment of electron-electron interactions within the linear response regime.
AI.result: At T=0.3Γ₀, the ring-chord geometry yields ZT ≈ 12, reaches 62% of Carnot efficiency with output power 6.24 fW, and achieves a spin thermoelectric figure of merit ZsT ≈ 18 via spin-polarized injection and Zeeman splitting.
AI.conclusion: Microwave-driven engineering of Fano interference is an effective strategy for modulating spin-caloritronic behavior in multi-quantum-dot devices.

title: Designing Quantum Matter in Pyrochlore Iridates: A Perspective on Recent Thin-Film Advances
summary: The pyrochlore iridates R2Ir2O7 have emerged as a unique playground for exploring exotic quantum phenomena arising from the intricate interplay of strong spin-orbit coupling, electron correlations, and geometric frustration. While bulk crystals of these materials have revealed a rich landscape of correlated and topological states, recent breakthroughs in epitaxial thin-film synthesis and heterostructure engineering unlocked an entirely new dimension of discovery. This brief Perspective reviews recent advancements highlighting how new tuning knobs such as dimensional confinement, epitaxial strain, and interfacial coupling can be used to manipulate the delicate balance of competing interactions. We discuss several key discoveries enabled by this approach including the realization of the magnetic Weyl semimetal phase in (111) oriented films, strain-engineered magnetic multipolar orders, the emergence of a chiral spin liquid-like state in the quasi-2D limit, and the discovery of novel electronically anisotropic states at interfaces between pyrochlore iridates and other quantum materials, such as spin ice pyrochlores. These findings showcase that low-dimensional pyrochlore iridates provide ample opportunities for both theory and experiment to unravel, control and ultimately design novel quantum states of matter. We conclude by outlining key open questions and future directions ranging from the synthesis of new heterostructures to the application of advanced probes and the exploration of non-equilibrium phenomena.

AI.tldr: This Perspective reviews recent advances in epitaxial thin-film synthesis and heterostructure engineering of pyrochlore iridates R₂Ir₂O₇, highlighting how dimensional confinement, epitaxial strain, and interfacial coupling enable new quantum states such as magnetic Weyl semimetal phases, strain-engineered multipolar orders, chiral spin liquid-like states, and anisotropic interfacial electronic states.
AI.motivation: To showcase how epitaxial thin-film synthesis and heterostructure engineering of pyrochlore iridates provide new tuning knobs (dimensional confinement, strain, interfacial coupling) for discovering and controlling exotic quantum states that are not accessible in bulk crystals.
AI.method: Epitaxial thin-film synthesis and heterostructure engineering of pyrochlore iridates, employing dimensional confinement, epitaxial strain, and interfacial coupling as control parameters to manipulate competing interactions.
AI.result: Key discoveries include: (1) magnetic Weyl semimetal phase in (111)-oriented films, (2) strain-engineered magnetic multipolar orders, (3) chiral spin liquid-like state in the quasi-2D limit, and (4) novel electronically anisotropic states at interfaces with other quantum materials (e.g., spin ice pyrochlores).
AI.conclusion: Low-dimensional pyrochlore iridates offer rich opportunities for theory and experiment to understand, control, and design novel quantum states; future directions include new heterostructure synthesis, advanced probes, and non-equilibrium phenomena.

title: Quantum fluctuations and chaos in fully connected spin models
summary: We investigate beyond-mean-field dynamics in a fully connected $\mathrm{SU}(3)$ spin-exchange model, focusing on the interplay between chaotic dynamics and quantum fluctuations. Using the two-particle irreducible (2PI) effective action formalism, we derive equations of motion that systematically account for higher-order correlations generated by interactions, and demonstrate how quantum fluctuations can regularize chaotic dynamics displayed by macroscopic observables. Our results show that an accurate treatment of fluctuations is essential for describing macroscopic dynamics in quantum many-body systems and promote 2PI as a robust framework for connecting microscopic correlations to macroscopic nonequilibrium phenomena.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates beyond-mean-field dynamics in an SU(3) spin-exchange model, showing that quantum fluctuations—captured via the 2PI effective action formalism—can regularize chaotic dynamics in macroscopic observables, highlighting the importance of fluctuations for accurate macroscopic descriptions.
AI.motivation: To understand how quantum fluctuations affect chaotic dynamics in many-body systems beyond mean-field approximations, and to establish a rigorous framework connecting microscopic correlations to macroscopic nonequilibrium phenomena.
AI.method: The two-particle irreducible (2PI) effective action formalism is used to derive equations of motion that systematically incorporate higher-order correlations beyond the mean-field level.
AI.result: Quantum fluctuations can regularize (stabilize/suppress) chaotic dynamics in macroscopic observables, meaning mean-field predictions of chaos can be misleading without fluctuation effects.
AI.conclusion: Accurate treatment of fluctuations is essential for describing macroscopic dynamics in quantum many-body systems, and the 2PI framework is a robust tool for bridging microscopic correlations to macroscopic nonequilibrium behavior.

title: Real-time nuclear-electronic orbital time-dependent density functional theory with a constrained traveling proton basis
summary: Nuclear quantum effects and non-Born--Oppenheimer effects play a vital role in many chemical and biological processes, motivating the incorporation of such effects into dynamical simulations. In real-time nuclear--electronic orbital time-dependent density functional theory (RT-NEO-TDDFT), the electronic and nuclear densities are propagated numerically in time according to the time-dependent Schrödinger equation. In this framework, specified protons are treated quantum mechanically on the same level as the electrons. The classical nuclei can be propagated on the instantaneous NEO vibronic surface using Ehrenfest dynamics. A traveling proton basis (TPB) can be used to describe the dynamics of moving protons in conjunction with Gaussian-type protonic and electronic basis sets for each quantum proton. Herein, we present a constrained TPB (c-TPB) approach that ensures each protonic basis function center coincides with the corresponding proton position expectation value during the dynamics. This approach produces accurate nuclear--electronic quantum dynamics and rigorously conserves energy. We demonstrate the accuracy and stability of this approach for computing molecular vibrational frequencies as well as simulating excited-state intramolecular proton transfer and double proton transfer in the o-hydroxybenzaldehyde and [2,2$'$-bipyridyl]-3,3$'$-diol molecules. These applications show that the c-TPB method provides accurate dynamics, conserves energy, and is computationally efficient.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a constrained traveling proton basis (c-TPB) approach within RT-NEO-TDDFT to simulate nuclear quantum effects and non-Born-Oppenheimer dynamics, demonstrating accuracy, energy conservation, and computational efficiency for proton transfer processes.
AI.motivation: Nuclear quantum effects and non-Born-Oppenheimer effects are essential for many chemical and biological processes, motivating the need for dynamical simulations that incorporate these effects.
AI.method: A constrained traveling proton basis (c-TPB) method is developed within the real-time nuclear-electronic orbital time-dependent density functional theory (RT-NEO-TDDFT) framework, where each protonic basis function center is constrained to coincide with the proton position expectation value during dynamics.
AI.result: The c-TPB method produces accurate nuclear-electronic quantum dynamics, rigorously conserves energy, and is computationally efficient. It is validated for computing molecular vibrational frequencies and simulating excited-state intramolecular proton transfer and double proton transfer in o-hydroxybenzaldehyde and [2,2'-bipyridyl]-3,3'-diol.
AI.conclusion: The c-TPB approach provides accurate dynamics, conserves energy, and is computationally efficient for simulating proton transfer processes and molecular vibrations.

title: Overcoming contact resistance at metal-2D semiconductor interfaces: atomically clean MoS2/Au ohmic junctions
summary: The application of two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors, such as monolayer MoS2, is limited by the high contact resistance commonly attributed to interfacial barriers at metal contacts. Furthermore, the dependence of electrical conductivity on MoS2 thickness is still unsettled, as both increasing and decreasing trends with layer number have been reported. By showing the contrast between electrical transport of mono- and multilayer MoS2 exfoliated on Au under ultra-high vacuum (UHV) and ambient conditions, we experimentally prove that, contrary to the prevailing view in the literature, the intrinsic MoS2/Au junction is highly conductive and exhibits ohmic behaviour. Our results indicate that interfacial contamination is responsible for the high contact resistances reported to date and affects the thickness dependence of electrical transport, explaining the discrepancies observed in the literature. We rationalize those findings using electrical transport simulations. Lastly, we show that local force-mediated lamination on lightly contaminated contacts can recover pristine, ohmic contacts, offering a route towards nanoscale patterning.

AI.tldr: MoS₂/Au contact resistance is intrinsically ohmic under UHV; interfacial contamination causes the high contact resistances and conflicting thickness-dependent conductivity trends reported in literature.
AI.motivation: To resolve the controversy around high contact resistance in 2D semiconductor (e.g., MoS₂) devices and the conflicting reports on how electrical conductivity scales with MoS₂ layer thickness.
AI.method: Comparative electrical transport measurements of mono- and multilayer MoS₂ exfoliated on Au under ultra-high vacuum (UHV) vs. ambient conditions, supported by electrical transport simulations.
AI.result: Intrinsic MoS₂/Au junction is highly conductive and ohmic; interfacial contamination (not intrinsic physics) causes the high contact resistances and the confusing thickness-dependent conductivity trends reported previously.
AI.conclusion: Contamination, not the MoS₂-metal interface itself, is the root cause of poor contacts. Local force-mediated lamination can recover pristine ohmic contacts on lightly contaminated samples, enabling nanoscale patterning.

title: Weak first-order phase transition out of the classical kagome spin liquid
summary: The low-temperature fate of the spin-liquid regime in the classical kagome Heisenberg antiferromagnet has been debated for over three decades.
